scenario_text: Patient presents in emergency complaining of low-grade pain on tooth 4.1, restored years ago. Periapical radiograph shows probing depths of 2 to 3mm and no periapical radiolucency.
task_instruction: Discuss treatment options with the patient.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient an opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances if applicable
Discusses fees

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Summarizes the problems with tooth 4.1
Provides more than one complete treatment option
Explains the advantages and disadvantages of the different options and identifies the preferred option
Verifies the patient understands the explanations
Communicates the information effectively and in an organized manner

critical_errors: Fails to disclose that tooth 4.1 requires further evaluation or treatment
Recommends extraction without discussing any restorative alternative
Provides no treatment option at all
model_answer: I want to walk you through what I found with tooth 4.1, your lower front tooth that was restored a while ago. The good news is the x-ray does not show any infection at the root tip, and your gum probing depths are normal at 2 to 3mm, so this does not look like an emergency requiring immediate root canal treatment. The low-grade discomfort you are feeling could be coming from the old restoration itself, possibly a small leak underneath it or a crack, or it could be mild sensitivity from the surrounding gum tissue. There are two reasonable ways we can move forward. The first option is to replace the existing restoration with a new one and monitor the tooth closely over the next few weeks to see if the discomfort resolves. The second option is to proceed directly to root canal treatment if you would rather address the nerve now rather than risk needing it later. The advantage of replacing the restoration first is that it is less invasive and less costly, and many times that alone resolves this kind of low-grade discomfort. The disadvantage is that if the nerve is already irritated, you might still end up needing root canal treatment down the road. Root canal treatment now is more definitive but is a bigger procedure with a higher cost, and it is not clearly necessary based on what I am seeing today. My recommendation is that we start with replacing the restoration and reassess in two to three weeks. Does that plan make sense to you, or do you have any questions about either option? We can also talk about the cost of each before you decide, and if there is anything specific about your schedule or health history I should know, please let me know now.

scenario_text: A 68-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes and a history of osteoporosis managed with oral bisphosphonates for six years presents needing extraction of a badly broken down tooth 4.6. She also has generalized moderate periodontitis and three small carious lesions noted on the bitewings.
task_instruction: Develop a problem list for this patient and explain your overall treatment sequence.
competent_behaviors: Reviews the patient's medical history in her presence
Explains why each problem was identified
Answers questions about medication risks in plain language

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies all active problems: non-restorable tooth 4.6, generalized moderate periodontitis, three carious lesions, and osteoporosis medication history
Recognizes the bisphosphonate history as a risk factor requiring modification of the extraction plan (medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw risk assessment)
Sequences treatment logically: address active disease and infection control before elective restorative work
Explains the rationale for the sequence to the patient in understandable terms

critical_errors: Proceeds to schedule the extraction without acknowledging or assessing the bisphosphonate history
Fails to identify the periodontal disease as an active problem
model_answer: Based on today's exam, I have identified a few things we need to deal with. Tooth 4.6 is broken down beyond what we can restore, so that tooth will ultimately need to come out. You also have generalized moderate gum disease affecting most areas of your mouth, and there are three small cavities on the bitewing x-rays that will need fillings. Before we go any further, I want to talk about the bisphosphonate medication you have been taking for your bone health for the past six years, because long-term use of that class of medication is associated with a risk of slow healing in the jawbone after extractions, so we need to plan the extraction carefully rather than just booking it as a routine procedure. My suggested order is this: first, we get your gum disease under control with a round of periodontal therapy, since active infection and inflammation make healing less predictable for everything else we do. Once your gums are healthier, we will address tooth 4.6, and depending on your specific bisphosphonate history I may want to consult with your physician beforehand to confirm the safest approach for that extraction. After the extraction site has healed, we will move on to the three cavities, which are not urgent right now. Does this order make sense to you? I am happy to answer any questions about how the medication could affect healing, and we can talk about cost for each phase as we get to it.

scenario_text: A 24-year-old patient presents with a chief complaint of sensitivity to cold on the upper right side. Clinical exam reveals a deep carious lesion on tooth 1.6 with no spontaneous pain, and a periapical radiograph shows the lesion approximating the pulp with no periapical pathology.
task_instruction: Explain the diagnosis and discuss treatment options with the patient.
competent_behaviors: Explains what causes cold sensitivity in plain terms
Offers the patient an opportunity to ask questions
Discusses fees for the options presented

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Establishes a working diagnosis of reversible pulpitis based on the absence of spontaneous pain and periapical pathology
Explains that the deep lesion places the tooth at risk of needing root canal treatment in the future
Presents restorative treatment (direct or indirect restoration) as the primary option
Discusses the possibility that root canal treatment could still become necessary despite treatment
Verifies the patient understands the diagnosis and the uncertainty involved

critical_errors: Recommends root canal treatment as the only option without discussing restorative treatment first
Fails to mention any risk that the pulp could become irreversibly involved
model_answer: The cold sensitivity you are noticing on the upper right is coming from a deep cavity in tooth 1.6. Because there is no lingering pain after the cold goes away and the x-ray does not show any infection at the root, this looks like what we call reversible pulpitis, meaning the nerve inside the tooth is irritated but still healthy enough to recover. My recommended plan is to clean out the decay and place a restoration, which in a deep cavity like this we would likely build up with a protective liner underneath before the final filling or crown, depending on how much healthy tooth structure remains once the decay is removed. I do want to be upfront that because this decay is close to the nerve, there is a chance the nerve could become more irritated even after treatment, and if that happens you might still need root canal treatment later. That is not the expectation, but I want you to know it is a possibility so it is not a surprise if symptoms return. Do you have any questions about why this is happening or what the procedure involves? Once you decide, we can go over the cost of the restoration and, if it comes to that later, what root canal treatment would cost as well.

scenario_text: A patient presents for a comprehensive exam and reports no complaints. Examination reveals four carious lesions of varying sizes (teeth 1.4, 2.6, 3.6, and 4.7), moderate generalized calculus, and a fractured cusp on tooth 1.7 that is asymptomatic but has a visible crack line extending into dentin.
task_instruction: Establish a problem list and propose a treatment sequence, prioritizing appropriately.
competent_behaviors: Explains findings tooth by tooth in a clear order
Gives the patient a chance to ask questions about priorities

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies all active problems: four carious lesions, generalized calculus, and the cracked cusp on tooth 1.7
Recognizes the cracked cusp on tooth 1.7 as the highest-priority restorative concern due to fracture risk
Recommends a periodontal cleaning as part of the initial phase to address the calculus
Sequences the largest and most at-risk carious lesions before smaller, more stable ones
Explains the rationale for prioritizing tooth 1.7 and the largest lesions first
Confirms the patient agrees with the proposed sequence before concluding

critical_errors: Fails to identify the cracked cusp on tooth 1.7 as a problem requiring treatment
Proposes an order that treats the smallest, least urgent lesion before the cracked tooth
model_answer: Today's exam found a few things I want to go over with you, even though you are not having any pain right now. First, tooth 1.7 has a crack running through one of the cusps that extends down into the deeper layer of the tooth. It is not bothering you yet, but cracks like this can propagate under chewing pressure, so I consider that our top priority even though it is symptom-free. You also have four cavities, on teeth 1.4, 2.6, 3.6, and 4.7, and they vary in size. Finally, you have a moderate build-up of calculus, or hardened plaque, around most of your teeth, which needs a professional cleaning to prevent it from progressing to gum disease. Here is how I would like to sequence things. First, we will get a cleaning done to address the calculus and give us a clean baseline. Second, we will restore tooth 1.7, since protecting that cracked cusp before it potentially breaks is the most time-sensitive item. Third, we will move to the larger of your four cavities, and finish with the smaller ones, since the bigger lesions carry more risk of reaching the nerve if we wait. Does that order work for you, or would you like to prioritize anything differently based on how you're feeling day to day? We can also go through the cost for each step whenever you are ready.

scenario_text: A 45-year-old new patient transfers care after her previous dentist retired. She brings old radiographs showing tooth 2.5 was root canal treated eight years ago with a temporary filling that was never replaced with a permanent crown. The tooth is now asymptomatic but the temporary material is worn thin in the centre.
task_instruction: Explain your findings and discuss the treatment plan for this tooth.
competent_behaviors: Reviews the patient's transferred records and history with her
Gives the patient an opportunity to ask questions
Discusses her special circumstance of not having had this addressed for eight years

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies the worn temporary restoration on a root canal treated tooth as an active problem needing definitive treatment
Explains the risk of fracture or recurrent decay if a permanent crown is not placed
Recommends definitive crown restoration as the appropriate next step
Verifies the patient understands why the temporary was never meant to be permanent

critical_errors: Fails to recommend any definitive restoration for the root canal treated tooth
Tells the patient the tooth requires no further treatment
model_answer: Thank you for bringing your old records and x-rays, they are very helpful. Looking at tooth 2.5, I can see it had root canal treatment done about eight years ago, and it looks like a temporary filling was placed afterward that was meant to hold things over until a permanent crown could be made, but that crown was never done. Right now the temporary material has worn quite thin in the middle, and root canal treated teeth without a permanent crown are at real risk of fracturing or allowing new decay to sneak in around the edges, since the temporary is not designed to seal or protect the tooth long term. My recommendation is that we move forward with a permanent crown on this tooth relatively soon, even though it is not causing you pain right now, precisely because the risk is silent until the tooth actually cracks. I understand this may have simply fallen through the cracks during the transition between dentists, and that is completely understandable, it happens. Do you have any questions about why a crown is needed at this stage rather than just a new filling? Once you're ready, we can talk about scheduling and the cost involved.

scenario_text: A patient presents with acute swelling and pain localized to tooth 3.7, which has a large carious lesion. Radiograph shows a periapical radiolucency approximately 5mm in diameter, and the patient reports the swelling started two days ago and is worsening, with slightly elevated temperature reported at home.
task_instruction: Explain your assessment to the patient and discuss the immediate and follow-up treatment plan.
competent_behaviors: Assesses the extent and firmness of the swelling before discussing treatment
Answers the patient's questions about what caused the swelling

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Establishes a diagnosis of acute apical abscess or acute periapical infection based on swelling, radiolucency, and systemic signs
Explains the need for urgent management, including drainage or access and possible antibiotics if systemic signs are present
Discusses definitive treatment options once the acute infection is controlled, such as root canal treatment or extraction
Advises the patient on warning signs that would require emergency hospital assessment
Verifies patient understanding of the urgency and the plan

critical_errors: Schedules elective, non-urgent follow-up without addressing the acute infection first
Fails to mention any warning signs of a spreading infection requiring emergency care
model_answer: Based on the swelling around tooth 3.7, the x-ray showing infection at the root tip, and the mild fever you mentioned, this looks like an acute dental abscess, which is an infection that has spread from inside the tooth out to the surrounding bone and soft tissue. Because you have some systemic signs like the elevated temperature, this needs to be dealt with today rather than waiting. My immediate plan is to get access into the tooth to allow the infection to drain, which relieves pressure and pain quickly, and depending on how things look once we open it up, I may also prescribe antibiotics to help control the spread of infection. Once the acute infection has settled down over the next several days, we will move on to definitive treatment, which will most likely be root canal treatment to save the tooth, or extraction if the tooth cannot reasonably be saved. I also want you to know what to watch for at home. If you notice the swelling spreading toward your eye or down your neck, if you have trouble swallowing or breathing, or if your fever gets significantly worse, you need to go to the emergency room right away, because that can indicate the infection is spreading beyond what we can manage here. Does all of that make sense? I want to make sure you know both the plan for today and what would be a red flag before we finish up.

scenario_text: A 16-year-old patient presents for a routine check-up accompanied by a parent. Radiographs show all four third molars (1.8, 2.8, 3.8, 4.8) are unerupted but developing normally with adequate space anticipated, and no pathology is present.
task_instruction: Discuss the findings regarding the third molars with the patient and parent.
competent_behaviors: Addresses both the patient and the parent appropriately
Gives them an opportunity to ask questions

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains the current developmental status of the third molars and the absence of pathology
Recommends a monitoring approach rather than immediate extraction, given the lack of any active problem
Explains what future signs or changes would prompt intervention
Confirms both patient and parent understand the plan to reassess at future visits

critical_errors: Recommends immediate extraction of asymptomatic, pathology-free, normally developing third molars without justification
Fails to discuss any plan for future monitoring
model_answer: I looked closely at the x-rays today, and all four wisdom teeth are still developing under the gums. At this stage they appear to have enough room to potentially come in normally, and there is no sign of infection, cysts, or crowding problems around any of them right now. Because everything looks stable and there is no active issue, my recommendation is that we do not remove them at this point, and instead we monitor their development at future check-ups with periodic x-rays. Things we would watch for going forward include signs of insufficient space as the jaw finishes growing, recurrent infection or gum irritation around a partially erupted tooth, cyst formation, or crowding of the neighbouring teeth, any of which would be reasons to reconsider extraction later on. Do either of you have any questions about wisdom teeth in general, or about why we are choosing to wait rather than remove them now? We will keep an eye on them at your regular visits and revisit this conversation if anything changes.

scenario_text: A patient with a complex medical history including a recent myocardial infarction three months ago presents requesting elective extraction of an asymptomatic, non-restorable retained root on tooth 1.8. The patient reports feeling generally well but is still on dual antiplatelet therapy.
task_instruction: Discuss your assessment and treatment planning approach with the patient.
competent_behaviors: Reviews the cardiac history and current medications in a respectful, non-alarming manner
Answers questions about bleeding risk in plain language

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies the recent myocardial infarction and dual antiplatelet therapy as significant medical risk factors requiring assessment before elective surgery
Explains that elective procedures are often deferred for a defined period following a recent cardiac event
Discusses the need for medical consultation with the patient's cardiologist or physician before proceeding
Reassures the patient the tooth is not an emergency and can safely wait for medical clearance

critical_errors: Proceeds to schedule the extraction without acknowledging the recent cardiac event or antiplatelet therapy
Dismisses the medical history as irrelevant to dental treatment planning
model_answer: I appreciate you letting me know about your heart attack three months ago and that you are still taking your blood thinning medications. Because this retained root is not causing you any pain or infection right now, we have the luxury of taking a careful, cautious approach rather than rushing into an elective extraction. Recent cardiac events combined with dual antiplatelet therapy raise two separate concerns for me, one being your overall cardiovascular stability for any elective procedure, and the other being an increased risk of bleeding during and after the extraction. Because of that, before we schedule anything, I would like to reach out to your cardiologist or family physician to confirm you are medically stable for an elective dental extraction and to get their guidance on whether your medications need any adjustment beforehand, which is something only they can safely decide. I want to reassure you that this retained root has no infection and is not an emergency, so there is no risk in waiting the short time it takes to get that medical clearance. Do you have any questions about why we are taking this extra step, or about what the consultation process will look like? Once we hear back, we will schedule the extraction with the appropriate precautions in place.

scenario_text: A patient presents complaining that food constantly gets packed between teeth 2.6 and 2.7. Clinical exam and bitewing radiograph reveal an open, poorly formed proximal contact between the two teeth with an existing amalgam restoration on 2.6, but no caries and healthy periodontal tissue currently.
task_instruction: Explain the cause of the problem and discuss treatment options.
competent_behaviors: Demonstrates the food impaction area to the patient using a mirror or model
Discusses fees for the options presented

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Correctly identifies the open or defective proximal contact as the cause of food impaction
Explains the risk of future periodontal or carious problems if left uncorrected
Presents replacement of the amalgam restoration with contact re-establishment as the primary option
Discusses an alternative or adjunct such as improved home care and interdental cleaning in the interim
Verifies the patient understands why simply cleaning the area will not resolve the underlying cause

critical_errors: Attributes the food impaction entirely to poor oral hygiene without identifying the open contact
Recommends no treatment at all despite an identifiable correctable cause
model_answer: The reason food keeps getting stuck between your upper left teeth 2.6 and 2.7 is that the contact point between them, where the old filling on 2.6 meets the neighbouring tooth, has become open or poorly shaped over time, so there is a small gap that traps food every time you chew. The good news is that your gums in that area look healthy right now and there is no new decay, but if this is left alone, chronic food packing can eventually lead to gum inflammation or even a new cavity forming at that same spot. My recommended solution is to remove the old filling on 2.6 and replace it with a new restoration specifically designed to rebuild a tight, well-formed contact against tooth 2.7, which should stop the food from packing there. In the meantime, until we can get that scheduled, using floss or a small interdental brush at that spot after meals will help manage the symptom, though I want to be clear that will not fix the actual cause, only the new restoration will do that. Do you have any questions about why simply flossing more won't solve this permanently? We can talk about the cost of replacing that filling whenever you're ready to move forward.

scenario_text: A patient presents with a chief complaint of a loose upper front tooth. Clinical exam reveals grade 2 mobility on tooth 1.1 with 6 to 8mm probing depths and radiographic bone loss consistent with severe localized periodontitis. Adjacent teeth show minimal attachment loss.
task_instruction: Explain your diagnosis and discuss the treatment options for this tooth, including prognosis.
competent_behaviors: Explains the mobility grading and probing depths in terms the patient can understand
Gives the patient time to process the news before discussing options

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Establishes a diagnosis of severe localized periodontitis affecting tooth 1.1
Explains that the prognosis for tooth 1.1 is guarded to poor given the degree of mobility and bone loss
Presents both periodontal treatment aimed at retaining the tooth and extraction with replacement as viable options
Discusses replacement options such as an implant, bridge, or partial denture if extraction is chosen
Verifies the patient understands the uncertain prognosis regardless of which path is chosen

critical_errors: States the tooth has a good long-term prognosis without qualification
Fails to mention extraction as a realistic option given the severity of bone loss
model_answer: The looseness you're feeling in your upper front tooth, tooth 1.1, is because of significant bone loss around it from gum disease, which has affected this tooth much more severely than the teeth next to it. When I measured around the tooth, the pockets were quite deep, 6 to 8mm, and the tooth has what we call grade 2 mobility, meaning it moves noticeably when I test it. I want to be honest with you that the long-term outlook for saving this specific tooth is guarded to poor, given how much support it has already lost. That said, we do have two reasonable paths forward. One option is to attempt periodontal treatment, including deep cleaning and possibly localized periodontal surgery, to try to stabilize the tooth and keep it as long as possible, understanding that even with treatment it may not last indefinitely. The other option is to extract the tooth now, before it becomes looser or more uncomfortable, and replace it with either a dental implant, a bridge, or a removable partial denture, each of which has different advantages I am happy to go through with you. Whichever path you choose, I want you to know upfront that this tooth's prognosis is not great either way, and that is an important part of making this decision together. Do you have any questions about what periodontal treatment would involve, or about the replacement options if we decide to extract?

scenario_text: A patient in her third trimester of pregnancy presents complaining of gum bleeding when brushing and a localized area of enlarged, red gum tissue between teeth 1.1 and 2.1 that bleeds easily on contact.
task_instruction: Explain your findings and discuss the appropriate treatment plan considering her pregnancy.
competent_behaviors: Reassures the patient that gum changes in pregnancy are common
Answers questions about safety of dental treatment during pregnancy

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Establishes a diagnosis of a pregnancy-associated pyogenic granuloma (pregnancy tumour) between teeth 1.1 and 2.1
Explains that this lesion is typically benign and often related to hormonal changes and local irritants such as plaque
Recommends conservative management with professional cleaning and improved oral hygiene as the initial approach during pregnancy
Explains that surgical removal, if needed, is generally deferred unless the lesion is bleeding excessively, is painful, or interferes with function
Discusses that the lesion often regresses after delivery once hormone levels return to normal

critical_errors: Recommends immediate surgical excision without discussing conservative management first
Tells the patient the lesion is unrelated to pregnancy without further evaluation
model_answer: What you're describing, the bleeding gums and that red, enlarged area of tissue between your two front teeth, is a condition sometimes called a pregnancy tumour, though the word tumour sounds much scarier than what it actually is, it is a benign, non-cancerous overgrowth of gum tissue that some people develop during pregnancy because of hormonal changes combined with local irritation from plaque buildup. Given that you are in your third trimester, my first recommendation is a conservative approach: a thorough professional cleaning to remove the plaque and calculus contributing to it, along with reinforcing gentle but effective brushing and flossing at home, which often helps the tissue calm down on its own. Routine cleanings and gentle procedures like this are considered safe throughout pregnancy, including in the third trimester. If the area continues to bleed heavily, becomes painful, or interferes with your ability to eat or speak comfortably, surgical removal is an option, but we would generally prefer to hold off on that unless it becomes necessary, since these lesions very often shrink or disappear on their own after delivery once your hormone levels settle back down. Do you have any concerns about dental treatment being safe during pregnancy in general? We can keep monitoring this together at your visits and revisit surgery only if it becomes truly needed.

scenario_text: A patient presents for a new patient exam with generalized wear on the incisal and occlusal surfaces of most teeth, most pronounced on teeth 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, and 4.1, with flattened incisal edges. The patient reports frequent morning jaw soreness and headaches, and her partner has mentioned she grinds her teeth at night.
task_instruction: Establish a diagnosis and discuss the treatment plan with the patient.
competent_behaviors: Asks about stress levels and sleep quality in a non-judgmental way
Gives the patient an opportunity to ask questions

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Establishes a diagnosis of bruxism based on the wear pattern, jaw soreness, headaches, and reported grinding
Explains the relationship between nocturnal grinding and the morning symptoms she is experiencing
Recommends a nightguard as the primary protective treatment option
Discusses monitoring the worn teeth for progression and addressing restorative needs only if wear becomes functionally significant

critical_errors: Recommends immediate full mouth restorative rehabilitation without first addressing the underlying bruxism
Fails to identify bruxism as the underlying cause of the wear pattern
model_answer: Looking at the wear pattern on your front teeth, especially 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, and 4.1, along with the jaw soreness and headaches you get in the mornings, and what your partner has noticed about grinding at night, this all points to a condition called bruxism, which is essentially clenching or grinding your teeth while you sleep, often without you being aware of it. The flattening we see on your teeth happens gradually over years from that repeated grinding force, and the morning jaw soreness and headaches are very classic symptoms of the muscle strain that comes along with it. My first recommendation is a custom nightguard, a removable appliance you wear while sleeping that cushions your teeth from that grinding force and helps protect them from further wear, and it often reduces the morning muscle soreness as well. As for the wear that has already happened, right now it does not appear to be affecting your bite or function significantly, so rather than jumping into extensive restorative work, I would prefer to monitor those teeth at your regular visits and only consider restorations if the wear progresses to the point where it is causing sensitivity, chipping, or bite problems. Do you have any questions about what causes grinding, or about how the nightguard is made and cared for? We will keep an eye on the wear together going forward.

scenario_text: A patient presents having recently been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and reports her blood sugar has been poorly controlled for the past several months. Oral exam reveals generalized moderate to severe periodontitis with multiple sites of 5 to 7mm probing depths and bleeding on probing, along with two small carious lesions.
task_instruction: Discuss the connection between her diabetes and her oral findings, and develop a treatment plan.
competent_behaviors: Discusses the bidirectional relationship between diabetes and gum disease in accessible language
Encourages continued communication with her physician about glycemic control

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies generalized moderate to severe periodontitis and two carious lesions as the active problems
Explains that poorly controlled blood sugar can worsen periodontal disease and that periodontal disease can in turn make blood sugar control more difficult
Recommends periodontal therapy as a priority given the active infection and its relationship to her systemic health
Sequences the carious lesions after or alongside periodontal therapy rather than as the sole focus
Encourages closer recall intervals given her current risk status

critical_errors: Fails to identify the periodontal disease as an active problem requiring treatment
Dismisses any connection between her diabetes and her oral health
model_answer: Thank you for letting me know about your recent diabetes diagnosis and that your blood sugar control has been challenging lately. That is actually very relevant to what I'm finding in your mouth today, because there is a well established two way relationship between diabetes and gum disease. When blood sugar is poorly controlled, it makes it harder for your body to fight off the bacteria causing gum infection, so gum disease tends to be worse and harder to treat, and at the same time, having active gum infection can make it more difficult for your body to control blood sugar levels, so each condition can make the other one worse. Right now you have moderate to severe gum disease throughout your mouth, with several areas showing deeper pockets and bleeding, and you also have two small cavities. Given the relationship between your gum health and your diabetes management, I would like to prioritize periodontal treatment first, since getting that infection under control could genuinely help both your mouth and your overall blood sugar control. We can address the two cavities either during the same phase or shortly after, they are not urgent enough to delay the periodontal work. I would also like to see you more frequently for cleanings and monitoring than we might otherwise recommend, given your current risk level. Do you have any questions about how gum disease and diabetes affect each other? I would also encourage you to keep working closely with your physician on your blood sugar control alongside the treatment we do here.

scenario_text: A patient presents complaining of a persistent bad taste and mild discomfort around tooth 3.6, which has a large, deep amalgam restoration placed approximately fifteen years ago. Radiograph shows recurrent decay at the margins of the restoration extending toward the pulp, with no periapical pathology.
task_instruction: Explain the finding and discuss treatment options with the patient.
competent_behaviors: Explains what recurrent decay means and why it can develop under an old restoration
Discusses fees for the options presented

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Establishes a diagnosis of recurrent caries around the existing restoration on tooth 3.6
Explains the bad taste is likely related to bacterial byproducts from the decay
Presents removal of decay and restoration replacement as the primary treatment option
Discusses the possibility that root canal treatment may be needed if decay is found to involve the pulp once removed
Verifies the patient understands the plan may change depending on what is found during treatment

critical_errors: Recommends no treatment despite radiographic evidence of decay approaching the pulp
States definitively that root canal treatment will not be needed without qualification
model_answer: The bad taste and mild discomfort you're noticing around tooth 3.6 are being caused by new decay that has developed underneath and around the edges of your old filling, which was placed about fifteen years ago. This is called recurrent decay, and it happens when the seal between the filling and the tooth breaks down over time, allowing bacteria to sneak in underneath, which is often what causes that unpleasant taste, since bacteria produce byproducts as they break down tooth structure. The x-ray shows this decay extending fairly close to the nerve of the tooth. My recommended plan is to remove the old filling along with all of the new decay and place a new restoration. I do want to prepare you for the possibility that once we get in there and remove all the decay, if it turns out the nerve has been affected, we may need to proceed with root canal treatment instead of, or in addition to, a simple filling, we won't know for certain until we see how deep the decay actually goes. Does that make sense? I want you to know the plan could shift once we're actually working on the tooth, and we'll talk through it with you at that point if it does. We can also go over the cost for a straightforward filling replacement compared to root canal treatment, so you have an idea of both possibilities ahead of time.

scenario_text: A patient presents with a chipped and slightly discoloured tooth 2.1 following a minor fall two days ago. The tooth is not mobile, responds normally to cold testing, and radiograph shows no root fracture or periapical changes, with a small enamel chip visible clinically.
task_instruction: Explain your assessment and discuss the treatment plan for this tooth.
competent_behaviors: Reassures the patient about the encouraging vitality test results
Gives the patient an opportunity to ask questions about esthetic options

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Establishes that the tooth is currently vital based on the normal cold test response and lack of mobility or radiographic findings
Recommends monitoring the tooth's vitality over time given the recent trauma, since changes can develop later
Presents a conservative esthetic option such as bonding or contouring to repair the chip
Explains follow-up testing at future intervals to monitor for delayed pulpal changes or discolouration progression

critical_errors: Recommends root canal treatment immediately despite normal vitality testing and no radiographic pathology
Fails to recommend any follow-up monitoring after recent dental trauma
model_answer: It's good news that after your fall two days ago, when I tested tooth 2.1 with cold, it responded normally, which suggests the nerve inside the tooth is currently alive and healthy, and the x-ray does not show any fracture of the root or changes at the tip of the root either. That said, because this was a traumatic injury, I do want to keep a close eye on this tooth over the coming months, since sometimes changes to the nerve can show up later even when everything looks fine in the first few days after an injury. For the chip and slight discolouration you're noticing right now, the most conservative option is a tooth-coloured bonding procedure, where we smooth and rebuild the chipped area to match the rest of your tooth, which is a relatively simple, reversible procedure that restores both the shape and appearance. Going forward, I'd like to see you back for follow-up vitality testing and an x-ray at a few set intervals over the next year, just to make sure the nerve stays healthy and there is no delayed damage from the trauma. Do you have any questions about the bonding procedure, or about what we'd be watching for at the follow-up visits? If anything changes, like new pain or increasing discolouration, please call us right away rather than waiting for the scheduled follow-up.

scenario_text: A patient with a long-standing anterior open bite presents wanting to address chronic difficulty biting into food and speech concerns. Clinical exam confirms a 4mm anterior open bite from canine to canine, with otherwise healthy teeth and gums and no active decay.
task_instruction: Discuss the diagnosis and the range of treatment options, including their scope and limitations.
competent_behaviors: Listens to the patient's specific functional and speech concerns before presenting options
Gives the patient an opportunity to ask questions

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Establishes the diagnosis of anterior open bite malocclusion as the cause of the functional and speech difficulties
Explains that orthodontic treatment, potentially combined with orthognathic surgery depending on severity, is the definitive option for correcting the underlying skeletal or dental discrepancy
Explains that referral to an orthodontist or oral and maxillofacial surgeon is appropriate given the complexity of this case
Clarifies that restorative dentistry alone cannot correct the underlying open bite and would only address superficial concerns
Verifies the patient understands the scope of what can realistically be achieved with each approach

critical_errors: Recommends only restorative bonding or crowns as a complete solution for a 4mm skeletal or dental open bite
Fails to mention orthodontic or surgical referral as an appropriate option
model_answer: The difficulty you're having biting into food and the speech concerns you mentioned are both consistent with what we call an anterior open bite, which in your case measures about 4mm between your upper and lower front teeth when you bite together, meaning those teeth don't actually touch. The good news is your teeth and gums are otherwise healthy with no active decay, so we're really dealing with a bite alignment issue rather than a disease process. I want to be upfront that a gap of this size generally cannot be fully corrected with restorative dentistry alone, meaning simply bonding or capping the front teeth would not close this gap in a way that actually restores normal function, and could even create other problems if we tried to force it. The definitive way to correct an open bite like this is through orthodontic treatment, which realigns the teeth and jaws over time, and depending on how much of this is coming from your jaw bones themselves rather than just tooth position, you may also need to be evaluated by an oral and maxillofacial surgeon for a combined orthodontic and surgical approach. I would like to refer you to an orthodontist for a full evaluation, since they are best equipped to assess the extent of the problem and determine whether surgery would also be needed. Do you have any questions about what that referral process looks like, or about why restorative options alone wouldn't be enough here? Once we hear back from the specialist, we can talk about how your ongoing dental care here fits alongside that treatment.

scenario_text: A patient presents reporting that a temporary crown on tooth 4.6, placed two weeks ago at another office pending a permanent crown, has come off twice already and feels sensitive to hot and cold. The prepared tooth is visible and slightly discoloured, with no swelling and a normal periodontal exam.
task_instruction: Assess the situation and discuss the treatment plan with the patient.
competent_behaviors: Asks about the patient's timeline for the pending permanent crown
Gives the patient an opportunity to ask questions about what happens next

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies that the exposed, prepared tooth structure is the likely source of the sensitivity
Recommends re-cementing or fabricating a new, better-fitting temporary crown as an immediate priority
Explains that prolonged exposure of a prepared tooth increases the risk of sensitivity, bacterial contamination, and shifting of adjacent or opposing teeth
Advises the patient to follow up with the original office for timely placement of the permanent crown, or arranges continuity of care as appropriate

critical_errors: Sends the patient away with no interim solution for the exposed, sensitive tooth
Fails to address the risk of leaving a prepared tooth uncovered for an extended period
model_answer: It sounds like you've had a frustrating couple of weeks with that temporary crown coming off twice already. The sensitivity you're feeling to hot and cold makes complete sense, because right now the prepared tooth structure underneath is exposed, and without that temporary crown in place to protect it, hot and cold stimulation reaches the tooth much more directly than it normally would. The good news is there's no swelling and your gum exam around the area looks normal, so this isn't turning into an infection at this point, but I don't want to leave things as they are. My first priority today is to get a well fitting temporary crown back on that tooth, either by re-cementing the existing one more securely if it's still in good shape, or by making a new temporary if the old one is too worn or ill fitting, since leaving a prepared tooth exposed for an extended period increases the risk of ongoing sensitivity, bacteria getting into the tooth, and even the neighbouring or opposing teeth shifting into the space over time. Once that's taken care of, I'd strongly encourage you to follow up with your original office as soon as possible to get the permanent crown placed, since that temporary was never meant to last this long, and if there's a delay on their end, we're happy to help coordinate or see you again in the meantime to make sure the tooth stays protected. Do you have any questions about what's causing the sensitivity or what to expect going forward?

scenario_text: A patient in her second trimester of pregnancy presents with a chief complaint of acute, severe pain from tooth 3.6, which shows deep caries and radiographic evidence of an acute periapical abscess with mild facial swelling.
task_instruction: Discuss the diagnosis and treatment plan, addressing her concerns about safety during pregnancy.
competent_behaviors: Reassures the patient that necessary dental treatment during pregnancy is safe when properly managed
Answers questions about medication and radiograph safety directly

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Establishes a diagnosis of acute apical abscess on tooth 3.6
Explains that this active infection needs prompt treatment regardless of pregnancy, since an untreated infection poses a greater risk than appropriate dental treatment
Confirms the second trimester is generally considered the safest window for necessary dental treatment during pregnancy
Discusses that any necessary radiographs or medications will be selected with appropriate precautions for pregnancy
Presents root canal treatment or extraction as the definitive treatment options for the abscessed tooth

critical_errors: Defers treatment of an acute abscess with facial swelling until after delivery
Fails to address the patient's safety concerns about treatment during pregnancy at all
model_answer: I know it can feel worrying to deal with a dental emergency while you're pregnant, so let's talk through this carefully. What you have is an acute abscess on tooth 3.6, meaning there is an active bacterial infection at the root tip that has caused the severe pain and the mild swelling you're noticing in your face. This is not something we can safely wait on, because an untreated infection actually poses more risk to both you and your pregnancy than appropriately managed dental treatment does, infection and the inflammation that comes with it are the real hazard here, not the treatment itself. The good news is that you're in your second trimester, which is generally considered the safest window during pregnancy for necessary dental procedures, since the first trimester carries more risk related to early development and the third trimester can be physically uncomfortable for lying back in the chair for a long time. Any x-rays we need will be limited to what's essential and taken with a lead apron and thyroid collar for protection, and if antibiotics or local anesthetic are needed, we will select options that have a strong safety record in pregnancy. Our two definitive treatment options going forward are root canal treatment to save the tooth or extraction if the tooth cannot reasonably be saved, and we can discuss both today once the acute infection is addressed. Do you have any other concerns about safety that I can address before we move forward?

scenario_text: A patient who wears a full upper denture and a partial lower denture presents complaining that the upper denture has become loose and uncomfortable over the past year, and that a lower back tooth supporting a clasp, tooth 3.7, was recently extracted at another clinic due to a fracture.
task_instruction: Assess the patient's needs and discuss a treatment plan addressing both prostheses.
competent_behaviors: Examines the fit and support of both existing prostheses before discussing solutions
Gives the patient an opportunity to ask questions about cost and timelines

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies the loose upper denture as likely related to ridge resorption over time
Recommends reline or remake of the upper denture to restore proper fit and retention
Recognizes that the loss of the clasp-bearing tooth 3.7 changes the support and retention needs of the lower partial denture
Recommends evaluation and likely modification or remake of the lower partial denture to accommodate the missing tooth
Sequences the two prostheses logically, addressing whichever is causing more functional impact first, or explains they can be managed concurrently

critical_errors: Addresses only the upper denture and ignores the impact of the extracted tooth on the lower partial denture entirely
Recommends no change to the lower partial denture despite the loss of a clasp-bearing abutment
model_answer: There are two separate things going on here that both need attention. First, your upper denture has become loose and uncomfortable over the past year, which is very commonly caused by natural resorption, or shrinking, of the bony ridge that the denture sits on, so the denture that once fit snugly no longer matches the shape of your gums as well as it used to. For that, my recommendation is either a reline, which adds new material to the fitting surface to improve the fit without remaking the whole denture, or if the ridge has changed significantly or the denture is older, a full remake may serve you better long term, and I'll be able to tell you which makes more sense once I take a closer look. Second, since tooth 3.7 was extracted recently and that tooth was holding one of the clasps for your lower partial denture, the partial has now lost one of its support and retention points, which means it very likely is not fitting or functioning the way it should anymore, even if you haven't noticed major problems yet, and continuing to wear it as is could risk further wear to the remaining teeth. I'd like to evaluate the partial closely and it will likely need to be modified or remade to properly account for that missing tooth. In terms of order, since the upper denture is bothering you the most right now, we can start there, and address the lower partial shortly after, or we can work on both around the same time if that suits your schedule better. Do you have any questions about timelines or the cost for either piece?

scenario_text: A patient presents six weeks after undergoing radiation therapy to the head and neck for oral cancer treatment, now in remission, reporting significant dry mouth and rapid development of decay at the gumline on multiple teeth, including 1.3, 1.4, 2.3, and 2.4.
task_instruction: Establish a problem list and develop a treatment and prevention plan appropriate for this patient's history.
competent_behaviors: Acknowledges the patient's cancer treatment journey with sensitivity
Answers questions about ongoing risk in a supportive manner

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies radiation-induced xerostomia as the underlying driver of the rapid decay pattern
Identifies the active carious lesions on teeth 1.3, 1.4, 2.3, and 2.4 as requiring prompt restorative treatment
Recommends high-concentration fluoride therapy and saliva substitutes or stimulants to manage the xerostomia
Recommends a significantly shortened recall interval given the ongoing high caries risk
Addresses caution around extractions in previously irradiated bone, noting the increased risk of osteoradionecrosis and the need for careful planning if extraction becomes necessary
Explains the plan clearly and confirms the patient's understanding of the ongoing risk

critical_errors: Fails to identify radiation-induced dry mouth as the cause of the rapid caries development
Recommends routine extraction of any affected tooth without acknowledging osteoradionecrosis risk in irradiated bone
model_answer: First, congratulations on completing your cancer treatment and reaching remission, that is a significant milestone, and I want to make sure we support your oral health carefully as you continue to recover. What's happening in your mouth right now, this rapid decay showing up at the gumline on several teeth, 1.3, 1.4, 2.3, and 2.4, is a very well recognized effect of radiation therapy to the head and neck, because radiation often damages the salivary glands, leading to significantly reduced saliva flow, or dry mouth. Saliva normally helps protect your teeth by washing away food debris, neutralizing acids, and providing minerals that strengthen enamel, so when saliva flow drops sharply, decay can develop very quickly, exactly what we're seeing here. My plan has a few parts. First, we need to restore the active cavities on those four teeth fairly promptly to stop them from progressing further. Second, to manage the dry mouth itself and reduce your ongoing risk, I'm going to recommend a prescription-strength fluoride toothpaste or gel for daily use, along with saliva substitute products or a saliva-stimulating rinse to help with comfort and protection between visits. Third, given how quickly decay is developing for you right now, I want to see you much more frequently than a typical six-month recall, likely every three months or even more often at first, so we can catch and treat anything new right away. One more important thing I need you to know: because you've had radiation to the jaw area, if we ever need to extract a tooth in the future, we have to be extremely careful and plan that very deliberately, since irradiated bone has a higher risk of a serious healing complication called osteroradionecrosis, so extractions are never treated as routine for you going forward. Does all of that make sense? Please don't hesitate to ask questions any time, this is going to be an ongoing partnership to protect your teeth.

scenario_text: A new patient transfers to your practice and, while taking a periapical radiograph on tooth 3.6, you notice the mesial canal on a root canal treatment completed by another dentist eighteen months ago was never obturated. The patient reports no pain and is unaware of any problem. The patient asks you directly what you see on the radiograph.
task_instruction: Discuss your findings with the patient, including how you will communicate professionally about the prior dentist's work.
competent_behaviors: answers any questions the patient asks
gives the patient an opportunity to ask questions
discusses the patient's special circumstances if applicable
discusses fees for any recommended further treatment

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: summarizes the radiographic finding factually (an untreated mesial canal) without speculating on the prior dentist's competence or intent
explains the clinical significance and the risk of future infection or symptoms if left untreated
presents more than one option, such as retreatment, monitoring with follow up radiographs, or referral to an endodontist
verifies the patient understands the explanation before proceeding
communicates information calmly, objectively, and in an organized manner

critical_errors: criticizes or disparages the previous dentist by name or implies incompetence or malpractice
refuses to discuss the finding with the patient
alters or backdates any record to imply the finding is new when it was in fact pre-existing without disclosure
model_answer: I would say to the patient: 'Looking at this new x-ray, I can see that on this root canal, one of the canals, the smaller one toward the middle of the tooth, was not completely filled to the end. This can happen because that canal system can be very small and hard to reach. Right now there is no sign of infection and you are not having any pain, which is good news. There are a few ways we can handle this. One option is to monitor it with a follow up x-ray in six to twelve months to make sure nothing changes. Another option is to have the canal retreated, either by me or by a root canal specialist, to clean and fill that missed canal properly. If it were left untreated and became infected later, you could develop pain or swelling and need retreatment at that point instead. Do you have any questions about what I have described? Given your situation, cost is something to keep in mind for either option. What are your thoughts on which direction you would like to go?' I would not comment on why the previous dentist missed the canal or suggest they did anything wrong, since I was not present and canal anatomy varies.

scenario_text: You are a general dentist employed as an associate. The practice owner tells you the schedule is tight this month and asks you to place an implant on tooth position 4.6, a procedure you have never performed independently and did not receive hands on training for in your equivalency program.
task_instruction: Respond to your employer regarding this request.
competent_behaviors: acknowledges the practice's scheduling and financial concerns
offers to help find an alternative solution
remains respectful and professional throughout the conversation
asks clarifying questions about timelines

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: clearly states that performing a procedure outside one's trained scope of competence is not something the candidate will do
explains the patient safety rationale, including the standard of care and duty to only perform procedures within demonstrated competence
proposes a constructive alternative, such as referral to an oral surgeon or periodontist, or arranging supervised training before attempting the procedure independently
communicates the refusal firmly but without being confrontational or accusatory toward the employer

critical_errors: agrees to perform the procedure despite lacking competence
agrees to perform the procedure without informing the patient of the candidate's limited experience
threatens or is verbally abusive toward the employer
model_answer: I understand the schedule is tight and that this is putting pressure on you. However, I have not been trained to place implants and have never done one independently, so I am not comfortable performing this procedure. Placing an implant without adequate training could put the patient at real risk and would also be outside my scope of demonstrated competence, which I have a professional obligation to respect. What I can do is refer this patient to an oral surgeon or periodontist I trust, and I can call today to see if they have room this month so we do not lose the patient from the practice. If you would like, I would also be glad to shadow or take a hands on course in implant placement so that in the future I could take on cases like this appropriately. I want to help solve the scheduling problem, just not by taking on a procedure I am not yet qualified to perform.

scenario_text: You co-own a small dental laboratory with your brother-in-law. A patient needs a crown on tooth 2.6 and you would normally send all your lab work there. The patient asks where the crown will be fabricated and whether you get any personal benefit from that choice.
task_instruction: Respond to the patient's question about the laboratory arrangement.
competent_behaviors: answers any follow up questions the patient has
gives the patient an opportunity to ask further questions
remains calm and does not appear defensive
discusses fees for the crown

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: discloses the financial relationship with the laboratory honestly and clearly
explains that the patient is free to choose a different laboratory or seek a second opinion if they wish
reassures the patient with objective quality information, such as material standards or turnaround, rather than relying on the relationship alone
verifies the patient is comfortable proceeding before continuing with treatment

critical_errors: denies or conceals the financial relationship when directly asked
pressures the patient to proceed without addressing the conflict of interest concern
misrepresents the quality or credentials of the laboratory to secure the patient's consent
model_answer: That is a fair question and I want to be upfront with you. Yes, I have a financial ownership interest in the laboratory I typically use, along with my brother-in-law. I use that lab because I know the quality of their crowns firsthand and I have a good working relationship with the technicians, but I understand why my having a financial stake in it might raise a concern for you. You are absolutely free to ask me to send the case to a different laboratory of your choosing, or to get a second opinion from another dentist before we proceed, and that would not affect our relationship or your care here at all. If you are comfortable continuing with the lab I use, I am happy to show you examples of their previous work. What would you like to do?

scenario_text: You overhear your front desk receptionist discussing a patient's HIV status loudly in the open waiting room with another staff member, in a way that other waiting patients could clearly hear.
task_instruction: Address this situation with the receptionist and outline what you will do next.
competent_behaviors: checks in on the affected patient's wellbeing if they are still present
remains calm and non-confrontational in front of other patients
documents the incident appropriately
thanks the receptionist for their cooperation once corrected

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: privately and promptly addresses the breach with the receptionist away from patients and other staff
explains why the disclosure was a serious breach of patient confidentiality and privacy legislation
takes immediate steps to prevent recurrence, such as reviewing or reinforcing office privacy protocols
considers whether the affected patient needs to be informed of the breach and offered an apology
follows up to ensure staff training on confidentiality is reinforced going forward

critical_errors: ignores the breach entirely and takes no action
publicly reprimands the receptionist in front of patients, causing further disclosure of the patient's information
discusses the patient's diagnosis further with other staff who have no legitimate need to know
model_answer: I would first quietly ask the two staff members to step into the back office with me, away from the waiting room. I would say: 'I need to talk to you both privately about something I just overheard.' Once in private I would explain that discussing any patient's health information, especially something as sensitive as an HIV diagnosis, where other patients can hear is a serious breach of confidentiality and privacy law, and it could seriously harm the patient's trust in us and expose the practice to real risk. I would ask what led to the conversation happening in that location and remind them that these discussions must only happen in a private area with staff who have a legitimate clinical need to know. I would document the incident and the corrective conversation in an incident log. I would then check whether the patient was still in the waiting room and, if so, speak with them privately, apologize sincerely for what occurred, and reassure them of the steps being taken. Finally, I would schedule a short refresher session for the whole team on our privacy and confidentiality policy.

scenario_text: A patient you treated last week sends you a friend request on a personal social media account, and separately messages you asking whether the swelling they are experiencing after their extraction on tooth 1.6 is normal.
task_instruction: Describe how you will respond to both the friend request and the clinical question sent through social media.
competent_behaviors: responds promptly so the patient is not left waiting for clinical guidance
remains courteous and non-judgmental about the patient reaching out this way
documents the interaction appropriately in the patient's chart
offers alternative contact methods for future concerns

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: declines or does not accept the personal friend request, maintaining a professional boundary
explains to the patient why clinical concerns should go through the office phone line or a secure patient portal rather than personal social media
avoids providing a full clinical assessment through an unsecured, informal social media message
directs the patient to call the office or come in if the swelling is concerning, and provides appropriate general reassurance or red flag guidance in the meantime
documents that the patient contacted the office through social media and how it was redirected

critical_errors: accepts the personal friend request and continues an ongoing personal social media relationship with a current patient
provides a full clinical diagnosis or prescription instruction entirely through the informal social media channel with no follow up through the practice
ignores the patient's message about swelling entirely
model_answer: I would not accept the personal friend request, since I keep a clear boundary between my personal life and my professional relationships with patients. I would reply to their message through the same channel saying something like: 'Thank you for reaching out. For anything related to your treatment, it is best to contact our office directly at [office number] or through our patient portal, since that ensures your information stays secure and that our clinical team can properly document and follow up on your concern. Some mild swelling in the first few days after an extraction is common, but if you are noticing significant increasing swelling, fever, or worsening pain, please call the office right away or go to urgent care if it is after hours.' I would then document in the chart that the patient contacted me via social media reporting swelling, that I redirected them to the office line, and what general guidance was given, and I would flag the front desk to expect a possible call from this patient.

scenario_text: You determine that a patient's periodontal disease requires referral to a periodontist for surgical treatment on the lower left quadrant including tooth 3.6. When you check back two weeks later, you learn the front desk never sent the referral because they assumed the patient could not afford it.
task_instruction: Address this situation with your front desk staff and with the patient.
competent_behaviors: remains calm and constructive with staff rather than punitive
reviews the office's referral tracking process for gaps
thanks staff for flagging the cost concern even though the outcome was wrong
offers to help the patient explore payment or financing options

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: clarifies with staff that referral decisions based on assumed affordability must not override a clinical treatment plan without discussing with the dentist first
contacts the patient promptly to apologize for the delay and to send the referral without further delay
explains to the patient the clinical risk of the two week delay in referral for their periodontal condition
implements or reinforces a system to confirm referrals are completed and tracked going forward

critical_errors: blames the patient for the delay instead of addressing the internal process failure
does not contact the patient at all once the missed referral is discovered
falsifies the referral date to conceal the two week delay
model_answer: I would first speak privately with the front desk staff member: 'I understand you were trying to look out for the patient's finances, and I appreciate that you care about that, but referral decisions based on cost need to come back to me before a referral is skipped, because a delay can have real clinical consequences for the patient's periodontal health. Going forward, I would like all referrals to be sent within twenty four hours of being written, and if there is a cost concern, please flag it to me and I will discuss financing or payment options directly with the patient rather than having the referral not go out at all.' I would then call the patient myself: 'I want to apologize, there was a mix up in our office and your referral to the periodontist was not sent out when it should have been two weeks ago. I am sending it out today. Given your periodontal condition, it is still important that you be seen soon, and I also want to let you know we have options like a payment plan if cost is a concern for you, so please do not let that be a barrier to getting this care.' I would also set up a referral tracking log so this cannot happen silently again.

scenario_text: Your sister calls asking you to see her son, your nephew, today for a chipped front tooth, tooth 1.1, and asks that you 'squeeze him in ahead of your other patients' and 'not worry about a formal exam since you know his history.'
task_instruction: Respond to your sister regarding how you will handle seeing your nephew.
competent_behaviors: expresses genuine care and willingness to help a family member
communicates warmly while still being clear about professional standards
offers a realistic timeframe for being seen
checks whether this is a dental emergency requiring more urgent same day care elsewhere if the office is fully booked

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: explains that even for a family member, a proper clinical examination and complete chart documentation must still be completed
clarifies that scheduling will be handled fairly through the same booking process used for other patients, rather than displacing another patient without their agreement
discusses that treating close family members can create professional and personal complications and, if appropriate, whether referral to a trusted colleague might be more appropriate for objectivity
confirms informed consent will still be obtained just as with any other patient
communicates the decision in a way that preserves the family relationship

critical_errors: agrees to skip a clinical examination or proper chart documentation entirely because the patient is a family member
bumps another scheduled patient without their knowledge or consent to accommodate the family member
provides treatment to the nephew without obtaining proper consent from the parent
model_answer: I would say to my sister: 'Of course I want to help him, a chipped front tooth can be uncomfortable and I do not want him in pain. Let me check today's schedule for the first available opening, and if it is truly urgent I may be able to work him in between patients, but I cannot ask another patient to give up their appointment without their agreement. Whenever I do see him, I still need to do a full examination and take an x-ray if indicated, and document everything properly in his chart just like I would for any other patient, even though he is family. I will also need you, as his parent, to go through the normal consent process with me before we do anything. Honestly, because he is family, it might actually be a good idea for me to have one of my trusted colleagues do a second look alongside me, just so I am not the only one making decisions about a family member's care, but I am happy to be involved and get him seen as soon as possible.'

scenario_text: After completing a full mouth rehabilitation, a grateful patient presents you with an envelope containing a two thousand dollar gift card to a luxury store as a thank you gift.
task_instruction: Respond to the patient regarding the gift.
competent_behaviors: expresses genuine appreciation for the patient's gratitude
remains warm and avoids making the patient feel embarrassed
gives the patient the opportunity to discuss their feelings about the outcome of treatment
documents the interaction in the chart

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: recognizes that a gift of this significant monetary value raises a real conflict of interest and professional boundary concern
politely declines the gift or, if declining outright would cause offence, proposes a more appropriate and modest alternative such as a thank you note, a small token, or a donation to a shared charity
explains the professional reasoning behind declining a gift of this scale without making the patient feel their gratitude was inappropriate
ensures the patient continues to feel valued and that the relationship remains warm despite declining the gift

critical_errors: accepts the large gift without any consideration of the conflict of interest it creates
reacts in a way that shames or embarrasses the patient for offering the gift
accepts the gift in exchange for reducing the patient's outstanding balance or providing free future treatment as a quid pro quo
model_answer: I would say: 'Thank you so much, that really means a lot to me, and I am so glad you are happy with how your treatment turned out. I have to be honest with you though, a gift of this size is more than I am comfortable accepting, since it is important to me that our professional relationship never feels like it could be influenced by gifts, even with the best of intentions. What would mean just as much to me is a short note about how the treatment has changed things for you, or if you would like to do something, I would be honoured if you considered a donation to [a local charity] instead. Please do not take this the wrong way, I am truly touched that you wanted to do this, I just want to keep our relationship on solid professional footing.' I would document in the chart that the patient offered a gift of this value and that it was respectfully declined, along with the alternative suggested.

scenario_text: The practice owner instructs all associates to recommend a specific brand of whitening treatment to every new patient during their exam, 'regardless of whether they ask about it,' because the practice receives a bonus from the manufacturer for units sold.
task_instruction: Respond to the practice owner regarding this instruction.
competent_behaviors: acknowledges the legitimate business interests of the practice
remains respectful and professional in tone
offers to discuss whitening when clinically or aesthetically relevant to a patient
asks about the details of the manufacturer arrangement to understand it fully

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: explains that treatment recommendations must be based on individual patient need and informed clinical judgment, not a blanket sales policy
raises the ethical concern that recommending treatment to every patient regardless of indication, tied to a personal or practice financial incentive, risks overtreatment and compromises patient trust
states that if whitening is discussed, any financial incentive tied to the recommendation should be disclosed to the patient
proposes an alternative approach, such as only discussing whitening when it is clinically or aesthetically relevant and the patient expresses interest

critical_errors: agrees to recommend the product to every patient regardless of clinical indication in order to maximize the bonus
agrees to conceal the financial incentive from patients if directly asked
recommends the product to a patient for whom it is contraindicated in order to comply with the directive
model_answer: I understand the practice benefits financially from this arrangement, and I am not against mentioning whitening options when it is genuinely relevant to a patient. However, I am not comfortable recommending a specific product to every single patient regardless of whether they have expressed interest or whether it is clinically or aesthetically appropriate for them. Doing that could come across as, and would actually be, putting a financial incentive ahead of individualized patient care, and if a patient later found out we get a bonus for every unit sold without them being told, it could seriously damage their trust in the whole practice. What I would suggest instead is that I bring up whitening naturally when a patient's presentation makes it relevant or when they ask about cosmetic options, and if I do recommend it, I am comfortable being upfront that the practice has a relationship with this manufacturer. I want to support the practice, but not in a way that compromises how I make clinical recommendations.

scenario_text: You are scheduled to work alongside a fellow associate dentist this afternoon and notice they have slurred speech, an unsteady gait, and a strong smell of alcohol on their breath. They have a patient scheduled for an extraction on tooth 4.6 in twenty minutes.
task_instruction: Describe how you will handle this situation.
competent_behaviors: approaches the colleague privately rather than in front of staff or patients
remains calm and non-judgmental in tone
shows concern for the colleague's wellbeing, not only the immediate patient safety issue
documents the incident factually and objectively

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: prioritizes immediate patient safety by ensuring the colleague does not treat any patients while impaired
privately expresses direct concern to the colleague about what was observed, without accusing them outright of a specific diagnosis
arranges for the scheduled patient to be reassigned, rescheduled, or seen by another available dentist
informs the practice owner or appropriate supervisor of the situation so it can be properly managed
recognizes the professional and, where applicable, regulatory obligation to report a colleague who may be practicing while impaired

critical_errors: allows the colleague to proceed with the extraction despite the signs of impairment
ignores the situation entirely and takes no action
publicly confronts or humiliates the colleague in front of patients or other staff
model_answer: I would first pull my colleague aside privately, away from staff and patients, and say: 'I am concerned about you right now, I am noticing some things that make me worried you might not be in a state to safely treat patients this afternoon. I care about you and I want to make sure both you and your patients are safe.' Regardless of how that conversation goes, I would not allow them to proceed with the extraction. I would immediately arrange for their patient to be rescheduled or seen by another available dentist, and explain to the front desk only that there has been a scheduling change, without disclosing the reason to staff who do not need to know. I would then inform the practice owner directly about what I observed so the situation can be addressed appropriately, including arranging for the colleague to get home safely rather than drive. I recognize that as a regulated professional I have an obligation to help protect patients from a potentially impaired practitioner, and depending on how the situation develops, this may also need to be reported to the regulatory college if the impairment is not addressed. I would document exactly what I observed and the actions I took, factually and without speculation.

scenario_text: A former patient posts a one star online review naming you and stating you 'botched' their crown on tooth 2.6 and left them in pain for weeks. You know from their chart that they missed two follow up appointments after voicing minor sensitivity.
task_instruction: Describe how you will respond to this online review.
competent_behaviors: remains calm and does not respond emotionally or defensively
considers whether to respond publicly at all versus reaching out privately
reflects on whether any genuine care improvement is warranted
consults practice policy or a colleague before responding if unsure

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: does not disclose any specific patient health information, treatment details, or appointment history in the public response
responds, if at all, with a brief, professional, and non-defensive general statement acknowledging the patient's concern and inviting them to contact the office directly
attempts to reach out to the patient privately, such as by phone, to address their concerns directly and offer to see them again
