avoids disparaging the patient publicly or suggesting they were at fault for missing appointments

critical_errors: publicly reveals the patient's private treatment details, appointment history, or health information in the response, violating confidentiality
responds publicly in an angry, defensive, or disparaging manner toward the patient
denies the patient care or retaliates against them in any way as a result of the review
model_answer: I would not reply publicly with any details about their treatment, their missed appointments, or anything else from their chart, since posting that information online, even to defend myself, would be a serious breach of patient confidentiality and could also violate privacy legislation. If I chose to respond publicly at all, I would keep it brief and professional, something like: 'I am sorry to hear you were not satisfied with your experience. Patient privacy prevents me from discussing details here, but I would welcome the chance to talk directly. Please call our office so we can address your concerns.' More importantly, I would try to call the patient directly and privately to say: 'I saw your review and I want to understand what has been going on and see how I can help. I noticed you had some sensitivity after the crown, and I would really like to have you come back in so I can take a look and make sure everything is as it should be.' I would not blame them publicly or privately for missing their follow up appointments, and I would use this as an opportunity to genuinely re-engage them in their care.

scenario_text: You realize, three weeks after the fact, that you forgot to document the informed consent discussion you had before extracting tooth 1.8 on a patient. A colleague suggests you simply add a note to the chart today but backdate it to the day of the procedure.
task_instruction: Respond to your colleague's suggestion and describe how you will handle the missing documentation.
competent_behaviors: thanks the colleague for raising the concern about the gap in documentation
remains calm and does not become defensive about the error
reviews what actually happened during the original consent conversation as accurately as possible
reflects on how to prevent this documentation gap in the future

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: declines to backdate the entry, recognizing that falsifying a record's date is a serious professional and legal violation
explains to the colleague why backdating undermines the integrity and legal validity of the record
adds the note to the chart today, clearly dated with today's date, explicitly stating it is a late entry describing the consent discussion that occurred on the date of the procedure
considers whether it is appropriate to follow up with the patient to confirm their recollection or address any outstanding questions

critical_errors: backdates the chart entry to make it appear the documentation was completed on the day of the procedure
fabricates details of a consent conversation that did not actually occur
leaves the chart with no record at all rather than adding a properly dated late entry
model_answer: I would tell my colleague: 'I appreciate you trying to help, but I am not comfortable backdating the note, because that would misrepresent when the documentation was actually made, and if this record were ever reviewed, for example in a complaint or legal matter, a falsified date could be a serious problem for me professionally and legally, on top of being dishonest.' Instead, I would go into the chart today and add a clearly dated entry with today's actual date, stating something like: 'Late entry, [today's date]: documenting consent discussion held with patient on [date of procedure] prior to extraction of tooth 1.8. At that time I discussed the diagnosis, the recommended extraction, the risks including but not limited to bleeding, infection, and nerve injury, the alternative of retention or referral, and the patient verbally consented to proceed.' I would write this as accurately as I can recall the actual conversation, without inventing details I am not sure of. Going forward, I would build in a habit of documenting consent immediately after each conversation, before moving to the next patient, to prevent this gap from happening again. Before closing the record, I would also consider whether it is appropriate to follow up with the patient directly, either by phone or at their next visit, to confirm my recollection of what was discussed matches theirs and to address any questions they may still have about the extraction, since that follow-up protects both the patient and the accuracy of my late entry.

scenario_text: A patient you have treated regularly for two years asks you out for dinner after their appointment, saying they have had feelings for you for some time.
task_instruction: Respond to the patient.
competent_behaviors: responds kindly and without embarrassing or humiliating the patient
maintains a professional tone throughout
reassures the patient that this will not negatively affect their ongoing care
gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions about the boundary being set

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: declines the invitation clearly and directly
explains that a romantic or dating relationship with a current patient would represent an inappropriate boundary violation and conflict of interest
clarifies that this decision does not reflect negatively on the patient personally and is about maintaining professional standards
discusses, if relevant, whether the patient would feel more comfortable transferring their care to a colleague going forward, without pressuring them to do so

critical_errors: agrees to begin a romantic or dating relationship with a current patient
responds in a way that shames, mocks, or humiliates the patient for expressing their feelings
threatens to discharge the patient from the practice as punishment for the disclosure
model_answer: I would say: 'Thank you for being honest with me, I know that was not easy to say. I am flattered, but I have to be clear that I am not able to have a romantic relationship with someone who is a current patient of mine. That kind of relationship would cross an important professional boundary and could really complicate the trust that needs to exist between a dentist and their patient. This does not change how I feel about continuing to provide you with good dental care, and I hope you will still feel comfortable coming to see me. If at any point you would feel more comfortable seeing a different dentist in the practice instead, that is completely okay too, and I would make sure that transition goes smoothly, but that is entirely your choice. Do you have any questions about what I have said?' I would keep the tone warm and respectful throughout so the patient does not feel embarrassed.

scenario_text: You overhear your dental assistant make a dismissive comment to a patient about their accent, saying 'I can barely understand what you're saying' in a mocking tone, right before the patient's appointment for a filling on tooth 4.7.
task_instruction: Address this situation with your assistant and with the patient.
competent_behaviors: checks on the patient's comfort before proceeding with treatment
remains calm and professional in front of the patient
documents the incident appropriately
reflects on broader practice culture around cultural competence

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: privately addresses the disrespectful comment with the assistant promptly, away from the patient
explains clearly why the comment was inappropriate and disrespectful and does not meet the practice's standard of care
apologizes to the affected patient on behalf of the practice
ensures the patient's treatment proceeds professionally despite the earlier incident
takes steps to prevent recurrence, such as a conversation about cultural competence expectations for the whole team

critical_errors: ignores the comment entirely and takes no corrective action
publicly humiliates the assistant in front of the patient in a way that further embarrasses the patient
allows the assistant to continue interacting with the patient in a demeaning manner during the appointment without intervening
model_answer: I would step in right away and quietly ask my assistant to step out for a moment, then turn to the patient and say: 'I am sorry about that comment, it was not appropriate and does not reflect how we want you to feel here. Are you doing okay to continue with your appointment today?' Once the patient's treatment for their filling on tooth 4.7 is underway or completed, I would speak privately with the assistant: 'What you said to that patient about their accent was disrespectful and unprofessional, and it is not something I can allow in this practice. Every patient deserves to feel respected regardless of how they communicate. I need you to understand why that comment was hurtful and that it cannot happen again.' I would document the incident and the corrective conversation. I would also use this as an opportunity to review cultural competence expectations with the whole team, so everyone understands the standard we hold ourselves to when interacting with patients from diverse backgrounds.

scenario_text: Your practice's dental hygienist asks you to sign off on a periodontal charting and scaling procedure for a patient you did not personally examine that day, since you were busy with another patient and she is confident everything is fine.
task_instruction: Respond to the hygienist's request.
competent_behaviors: acknowledges the hygienist's competence and trust in her clinical judgment
remains respectful of her workload and time pressures
offers a practical solution to avoid delaying the patient
thanks her for flagging that she needed a sign off at all

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: explains that signing off on a record for a patient the candidate has not personally examined that day would misrepresent the record and the candidate's own clinical oversight
declines to sign the chart without having reviewed the findings or examined the patient personally
offers a reasonable alternative, such as briefly examining the patient before the end of the visit, or reviewing the hygienist's findings together before the patient leaves
communicates the decision in a way that supports the hygienist rather than making her feel distrusted

critical_errors: signs off on the clinical record without having examined the patient or reviewed the actual findings at all
asks the hygienist to falsify the record to make it appear the dentist examined the patient that day
refuses to see the patient at all, causing the patient's care to be left incomplete with no plan to follow up
model_answer: I would say: 'I trust your clinical judgment completely, but I cannot sign off on this chart without having actually seen the patient or reviewed the findings myself today, since signing it would suggest I examined them when I did not, and that would not be an accurate record. Can I take five minutes to pop in and do a quick check, or walk through your findings with you before the patient leaves, so I can sign off properly?' If truly no time is available that day, I would say: 'If I genuinely cannot get to it today, let us have the patient booked back in soon so I can do a proper exam and sign off then, rather than signing something I have not actually reviewed.' I want to support her and keep things moving efficiently for the patient, but not at the cost of an accurate clinical record.

scenario_text: Your office manager suggests billing a patient's insurance for a full crown procedure code on tooth 3.6 when in fact a less costly buildup and large filling was performed, saying 'the insurance company won't know the difference and the patient needs the money covered.'
task_instruction: Respond to your office manager's suggestion.
competent_behaviors: acknowledges the office manager's intent to help the patient financially
remains calm and non-accusatory in tone
offers to discuss legitimate financial options with the patient
reviews the office's billing procedures to prevent similar suggestions in the future

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: clearly states that submitting an insurance claim for a procedure that was not actually performed constitutes insurance fraud
explains the serious professional, legal, and regulatory consequences of fraudulent billing for both the dentist and the practice
instructs that the claim be submitted accurately reflecting the actual procedure performed
proposes a legitimate way to help the patient with cost, such as a payment plan or discussing options directly with the patient rather than misrepresenting the procedure to the insurer

critical_errors: agrees to submit the insurance claim under an inaccurate procedure code
instructs staff to alter clinical documentation to make the record match the fraudulent billing code
threatens or intimidates the office manager rather than addressing the issue directly and professionally
model_answer: I understand you are trying to help the patient with the cost, and I appreciate that, but I cannot agree to bill the insurance company for a procedure that was not actually performed. Submitting a claim for a full crown when we actually did a buildup and large filling would be insurance fraud, and that carries serious consequences, both legally and for my professional licence, and it could put the whole practice at risk as well. What I can do is make sure the claim accurately reflects the buildup and filling that was actually done. If the patient is having trouble affording the difference, let us sit down with them and talk about a payment plan, or look at whether there are other coverage options, rather than misrepresenting what was done. I want to help this patient too, just not in a way that involves dishonesty with the insurer.

scenario_text: A colleague posts a before and after photo of a cosmetic case on their public social media account, including a clearly visible full face photo of the patient smiling, with no caption indicating consent was obtained.
task_instruction: Describe how you would address this with your colleague.
competent_behaviors: approaches the colleague privately rather than publicly commenting or reporting immediately
remains respectful and assumes good intent initially
acknowledges the value of sharing clinical work for professional marketing purposes when done properly
offers to help the colleague develop a proper consent process going forward

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: raises the concern that posting an identifiable patient photo without documented consent is a privacy and confidentiality breach
asks the colleague directly whether written consent was obtained from the patient before posting
recommends the post be taken down promptly if consent cannot be confirmed
suggests a proper process for future posts, such as written photo release consent forms and, where possible, using images that are not identifiable

critical_errors: takes no action despite recognizing the likely absence of consent
publicly shames or reports the colleague online rather than raising the concern directly and privately first
shares or reposts the same identifiable patient photo further, compounding the privacy breach
model_answer: I would message my colleague privately: 'Hey, I saw the before and after post you shared, the case looks great, but I noticed it includes a full face photo where the patient is clearly identifiable, and I did not see anything indicating you had their consent to post it publicly. Did you get written consent from them for that specific use?' If they had not obtained proper consent, I would say: 'I would strongly recommend taking that post down for now, since posting an identifiable patient's photo without documented consent is a real privacy and confidentiality issue and could put you at risk if the patient were to complain to the college.' I would then offer something constructive: 'Going forward, it might help to have patients sign a specific photo release form before you use their images anywhere public, or you could crop the photos so the patient is not identifiable if you do not have that consent. I am happy to share the consent form template I use if that would help.'

scenario_text: A patient needs a surgical extraction of an impacted tooth 3.8 that is beyond your comfort level, but tells you they cannot afford the oral surgeon's fee and asks if you would just do it yourself instead since you are cheaper.
task_instruction: Respond to the patient's request.
competent_behaviors: acknowledges the patient's financial concern with empathy
answers any questions the patient has about the referral
explores whether any financial assistance options exist
discusses fees openly and honestly

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: explains honestly that this specific extraction is outside the candidate's scope of comfort and training
explains the safety rationale for referral, including the risks of attempting a complex surgical extraction without adequate training or experience
helps the patient explore alternatives to manage the cost, such as payment plans with the specialist, dental school clinics, or public dental programs if eligible
verifies the patient understands the referral is being made for their safety, not to avoid helping them

critical_errors: agrees to perform the surgical extraction despite it being outside personal scope of competence, solely to accommodate the patient's cost concern
dismisses the patient's financial concern without offering to help explore any alternatives
misrepresents their own training or experience level to reassure the patient into proceeding
model_answer: I completely understand that cost is a real concern for you, and I do not want that to be a barrier to getting the care you need. However, I have to be honest with you: this particular extraction of tooth 3.8 is impacted in a way that is beyond what I am comfortable or trained to do safely. If I were to attempt it myself, there could be a real risk of complications like nerve injury or a difficult surgical situation I am not equipped to handle, and that risk is not worth taking to save money. What I can do is help you look at other options, such as asking the oral surgeon's office about a payment plan, checking whether a dental school clinic near you offers reduced fee oral surgery, or seeing if there are any public assistance programs you might qualify for. I want you to get this taken care of safely, and I am happy to help you find a way to make that possible.

scenario_text: An elderly patient with a documented diagnosis of moderate dementia arrives with her adult son for a scheduled extraction of tooth 1.7. The patient seems confused about why she is there and cannot clearly answer your questions about the procedure, while her son insists 'just go ahead, I already agreed to it for her.'
task_instruction: Respond to the son regarding how you will proceed.
competent_behaviors: shows respect and patience toward both the patient and her son
attempts to communicate directly and gently with the patient herself first
acknowledges the son's role and concern for his mother
documents the capacity assessment and consent process thoroughly

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: recognizes that the patient's apparent confusion raises a genuine question about her capacity to provide informed consent that day

explains that a family member's agreement alone does not substitute for the patient's own informed consent unless the son holds proper legal authority, such as a substitute decision maker or power of attorney for personal care
asks whether appropriate legal documentation of substitute decision making authority exists, and reviews it if provided
does not proceed with the extraction until proper consent, either from the patient with adequate capacity or from a legitimate substitute decision maker, is confirmed

critical_errors: proceeds with the extraction based solely on the son's verbal agreement without confirming the patient's capacity or the son's legal authority to consent
dismisses the patient entirely and directs all communication and decision making only to the son without attempting to include her
fails to document any assessment of capacity or consent at all before treatment
model_answer: I would first try to speak directly and gently with the patient herself: 'Hi, I am your dentist today, can you tell me what brings you in to see me?' If she cannot clearly demonstrate an understanding of the procedure, the risks, or why she is here, that raises a real concern about her capacity to consent today. I would then turn to her son and say: 'I understand you want to help your mother and that you agreed to this on her behalf, but I need to make sure I am following proper consent procedures, since her diagnosis of dementia means I have to carefully consider whether she is able to consent for herself today. Do you have legal documentation showing you are her substitute decision maker or that you hold power of attorney for personal care decisions?' If he has valid documentation, I would review it and, if appropriate, proceed with him providing substitute consent while still explaining everything to the patient as much as she can understand. If no such documentation exists, I would explain that I cannot proceed with an elective extraction today without proper consent in place, and I would help them understand what steps are needed, such as consulting the family physician or a legal advisor about substitute decision making, before treatment can move forward, unless this were a true emergency requiring urgent intervention.

scenario_text: A man calls your office identifying himself as the ex-husband of one of your patients and asks you to fax him her complete dental records, including a recent panoramic radiograph, saying he needs them for an ongoing custody dispute involving their children.
task_instruction: Respond to this request over the phone.
competent_behaviors: remains polite and professional despite the sensitive and potentially adversarial context
explains the general process for legitimate record requests
avoids making assumptions about the underlying custody dispute
documents the call in the patient's chart

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: declines to release any records or information without the patient's own explicit written authorization
explains that dental records are confidential and protected by privacy legislation, and cannot be released to a third party, including a former spouse, without proper consent
advises the caller of the proper channel for obtaining records if he believes he is legally entitled to them, such as through a court order or the patient's own signed release
notifies or plans to notify the patient that this request was made, so she is aware of the situation

critical_errors: releases any portion of the patient's records or radiographs to the caller without proper written authorization or a valid court order
confirms or denies that the caller's ex-wife is even a patient of the practice without a legitimate basis to do so
discusses any details of the patient's care or history with the caller over the phone
model_answer: I would say: 'I am not able to confirm or share any patient information over the phone, including whether someone is a patient here, without that patient's own written consent or a valid court order. Dental records are confidential and protected by privacy law, so I cannot release records to a third party based on a phone request alone, regardless of the circumstances. If you believe you are legally entitled to these records for the custody matter, you would need to obtain a court order requiring their release, or have the patient herself provide written authorization to our office.' I would not discuss anything further about the situation or the patient. After the call, I would document exactly what was requested and how it was handled, and I would contact the patient to let her know that someone identifying himself as her ex-husband called requesting her records, so she is aware and can take any steps she feels are necessary.

scenario_text: A new patient arrives for a comprehensive examination. During intake she states that, for religious reasons, she is not comfortable being examined by a male dentist and would prefer a female provider whenever possible. You are the only dentist working today and a male dental assistant is also present.
task_instruction: Respond to the patient in a way that demonstrates cultural competence while still meeting her clinical needs today.
competent_behaviors: Thanks the patient for sharing her preference openly
Offers to have a female staff member present as a chaperone during the visit
Answers any questions the patient has about today's visit
Asks if there is anything else that would make her more comfortable

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Acknowledges the preference respectfully without judgment or defensiveness
Explains realistically what accommodations are and are not possible today given staffing
Offers a concrete alternative, such as booking future routine visits with a female colleague if one is available
Confirms the patient's consent to proceed with today's visit under the agreed arrangement before starting

critical_errors: Dismisses or ridicules the patient's stated religious or cultural preference
Proceeds with the examination without addressing the concern or obtaining the patient's agreement to proceed
Refuses to treat the patient at all without offering any alternative or referral
model_answer: I would first thank her for telling me this directly, since many patients do not feel comfortable raising it. I would explain that I am the only dentist in clinic today, but that I can have my assistant, or another female staff member if available, remain in the room throughout the visit as a chaperone, and that I will keep the examination efficient and professional. I would let her know that for future routine visits I can try to schedule her with a female colleague if one is on staff, and ask whether that arrangement works for her today. I would answer any questions she has about the process, check whether anything else would help her feel more comfortable, and confirm she is willing to proceed before beginning the examination. Throughout, I would maintain a respectful, non-judgmental tone and avoid making her explain or justify her preference further than she already has.

scenario_text: A patient who recently immigrated to Canada speaks very limited English. His adult daughter, who is not a trained interpreter, has come with him to translate. The patient needs a detailed explanation of treatment options for a periapical abscess on tooth 2.6.
task_instruction: Communicate effectively with this patient given the language barrier.
competent_behaviors: Speaks directly to the patient, not only to the daughter
Uses simple, jargon-free language and short sentences
Checks in periodically to see if the daughter is translating accurately
Thanks both the patient and the daughter for their patience

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Asks the patient whether he would prefer to use a professional or telephone interpreter service rather than relying solely on a family member
Uses visual aids or a simple diagram to support the verbal explanation of the abscess and treatment options
Confirms the patient's understanding using teach-back, asking him or the interpreter to restate the plan in his own words
Documents that a family member interpreter was used and that the patient was offered a professional alternative
Verifies consent is genuinely the patient's own decision and not solely the daughter's decision on his behalf

critical_errors: Proceeds with treatment planning based only on the family member's summary without any attempt to confirm the patient's own understanding
Excludes the patient entirely from the conversation, speaking and deciding only with the daughter
Documents consent as obtained when there is no reasonable basis to believe the patient understood the explanation
model_answer: I would greet the patient directly and explain, through his daughter, that I want to make sure he fully understands his condition and options, and I would ask whether he would prefer a professional or telephone interpreter service rather than relying only on family for a decision this important. If he is comfortable continuing with his daughter, I would speak in short, plain sentences, pause often, and use a simple diagram showing the infected tooth and the treatment choices, root canal treatment versus extraction, including the advantages and disadvantages of each. I would periodically check with the daughter that her translation matches what I intended, and ask the patient to tell me in his own words what he understood the plan to be, so I can correct any gaps. I would document that a family interpreter was used, that a professional interpreter option was offered, and that the patient demonstrated understanding before I recorded his consent to proceed.

scenario_text: A new adult patient presents for a comprehensive oral examination. The medical history form is only partially completed. You notice he has listed a heart condition but has not specified which medications he takes.
task_instruction: Gather the information you need before proceeding with treatment planning.
competent_behaviors: Explains to the patient why detailed medical information is needed
Reassures the patient that the information is confidential
Thanks the patient for the information he does provide
Offers to help him contact his physician's office if he cannot recall details

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Asks open-ended questions to clarify the specific cardiac diagnosis, not just that a condition exists
Specifically asks about anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication use given the bleeding risk relevance to dental treatment
Asks about allergies, other medications, and any recent hospitalizations or procedures
Asks whether the patient requires antibiotic prophylaxis or has any activity restrictions from his cardiologist
Confirms he will obtain written medical clearance or a medication list from his physician before any invasive procedure if needed

critical_errors: Proceeds to plan an invasive procedure such as an extraction without clarifying the cardiac history and current medications
Fails to ask about anticoagulant use at all despite the incomplete history
Fabricates or assumes medical details rather than gathering them from the patient or physician
model_answer: I would explain to the patient that because he has noted a heart condition, I need a complete picture before planning any treatment, and that this information stays confidential in his chart. I would ask him to describe the specific diagnosis in his own words, for example whether it is a valve condition, a prior heart attack, or an arrhythmia, and then specifically ask whether he takes any blood thinners or antiplatelet medication, since that changes how I would manage bleeding risk for procedures. I would also ask about all other current medications, known allergies, and any recent cardiac procedures or hospitalizations, and whether his cardiologist has given him any restrictions or told him he needs antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work. If he cannot answer fully, I would offer to help him request a medication list or medical clearance letter from his physician, and I would hold off on any invasive treatment until that information is confirmed in writing.

scenario_text: A patient presents with a chief complaint of intermittent sharp pain on tooth 1.6 that started three days ago, worse with cold and chewing.
task_instruction: Take a focused history of the presenting complaint before beginning your clinical examination.
competent_behaviors: Uses a calm, unhurried tone while questioning
Allows the patient to describe the pain in his own words first
Thanks the patient for the detailed description
Explains that the history will guide the examination that follows

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Asks about the onset, duration, and frequency of the pain
Asks about quality and severity of the pain, such as sharp versus dull and a pain scale rating
Asks about specific aggravating and relieving factors, including cold, heat, chewing, and lying down
Asks whether the pain lingers after the stimulus is removed or resolves immediately
Asks about any associated symptoms such as swelling, fever, or a bad taste

critical_errors: Begins clinical testing or treatment without asking any history of the presenting complaint
Fails to ask any question that would distinguish reversible from irreversible pulpitis, such as lingering pain
Records history details that were never actually asked of the patient
model_answer: I would first let the patient describe the pain in his own words, then ask focused follow-up questions. I would ask when it started, how often it occurs, and whether it has been getting worse. I would ask him to rate the pain and describe whether it is sharp, dull, or throbbing. I would specifically ask what brings it on, cold, heat, sweet foods, or chewing, and what makes it better. A key question I would ask is whether the pain lingers for a while after the stimulus is removed or stops right away, since lingering pain suggests irreversible pulpitis while brief pain suggests a reversible cause. I would also ask about any swelling, fever, or bad taste in the mouth that might suggest an abscess. I would explain that this history helps me decide which clinical and radiographic tests to perform on tooth 1.6.

scenario_text: You are discussing a patient's treatment plan with your dental assistant at the front desk. Another patient sitting in the waiting area, only a few feet away, can clearly overhear the conversation, including the patient's name and diagnosis.
task_instruction: Address the situation appropriately to protect patient privacy.
competent_behaviors: Remains calm and professional rather than appearing flustered
Apologizes if the conversation was already partially overheard
Thanks the assistant for continuing the discussion appropriately afterward
Checks that the waiting patient was not distressed by what was overheard

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Immediately stops the conversation once the privacy risk is recognized
Moves the discussion to a private area such as an operatory or private office
Continues the clinical discussion only after privacy is restored
Reminds staff generally, not by singling anyone out publicly, about maintaining patient confidentiality in shared spaces

critical_errors: Continues discussing the patient's identifiable diagnosis and details within earshot of other patients after recognizing the breach
Discloses the overheard patient's information to the waiting patient or anyone else unnecessarily
Takes no corrective action at all despite recognizing the privacy concern
model_answer: As soon as I realize the conversation can be overheard, I would stop discussing any identifiable patient details right away and suggest to my assistant that we continue in a private area, such as an empty operatory or the private office, away from the waiting room. Once we are somewhere private, I would finish reviewing the treatment plan there. I would briefly check on the waiting patient to make sure they were not upset by what they may have overheard, without discussing the other patient's information with them. Afterward, I would use this as a general reminder to the team, not directed at any one person publicly, that clinical discussions involving patient names or diagnoses need to happen in private areas, to protect confidentiality for everyone who comes through the clinic.

scenario_text: A woman calls the office asking for details about her adult son's recent dental treatment, including his diagnosis and what he was charged. The chart shows no consent on file allowing information to be shared with family members.
task_instruction: Respond to the caller appropriately while protecting the patient's privacy.
competent_behaviors: Speaks to the caller politely and without sounding accusatory
Explains the general reason privacy rules exist, without being condescending
Offers to have the patient himself contact her office directly if he wishes
Documents the call and the response given in the patient's chart

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Declines to confirm or deny that the son is even a patient of the practice without his consent
Explains that information can only be released to a third party with the patient's documented consent
Offers to note the caller's request in the chart so the patient can be asked directly whether he wants to authorize disclosure
Does not disclose any clinical or financial details over the phone during the call

critical_errors: Discloses the patient's diagnosis, treatment details, or financial information to the caller without documented consent
Confirms the patient's identity as a patient of the practice and treatment details based only on the caller's assumed relationship
Promises to share the requested information without ever obtaining the patient's actual consent
model_answer: I would speak to the caller politely but explain that, without the patient's own consent on file authorizing us to share information with a family member, I am not able to confirm or discuss any details about his care, including whether he is even a patient here. I would explain that this is standard practice to protect every patient's confidentiality, not something specific to her son. I would offer to make a note that she called so that we can ask the patient directly, the next time we speak with him, whether he would like to authorize us to share information with her in the future. I would not disclose his diagnosis, treatment, or billing information during the call, and I would document the call, what was requested, and how it was handled in his chart.

scenario_text: You have diagnosed a symptomatic irreversible pulpitis on tooth 3.6 with complex canal anatomy that is beyond the scope of your practice. You need to refer the patient to an endodontist for root canal treatment.
task_instruction: Prepare the referral for the endodontist.
competent_behaviors: Explains to the patient why a specialist referral is recommended
Answers the patient's questions about the referral process
Discusses the approximate timeline and urgency of the referral with the patient
Confirms the patient's preferred contact information for the specialist's office

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Includes the patient's identifying information, tooth number 3.6, and the specific diagnosis in the written referral
Includes relevant clinical findings such as pulp testing results and probing depths
Attaches or references the diagnostic radiograph taken of tooth 3.6
States the reason for referral clearly, such as complex canal anatomy beyond the scope of general practice
Includes the referring dentist's contact information for follow-up communication

critical_errors: Sends a referral with the wrong tooth number or no tooth number at all
Fails to include any clinical rationale, making it impossible for the specialist to understand why the referral was made
Sends the referral without the patient's knowledge or agreement to be referred
model_answer: The written referral would read: 'Referral to Endodontics. Patient: [name, date of birth, contact information]. Tooth 3.6. Diagnosis: symptomatic irreversible pulpitis with normal periapical tissues. Clinical findings: lingering pain to cold, positive percussion, probing depths within normal limits. Radiograph enclosed showing complex, curved mesial canal anatomy. Reason for referral: canal anatomy assessed as beyond the scope of general practice; endodontic treatment recommended. Referring dentist: [name and contact information]. Please advise of findings and treatment outcome for continuity of care.' Before sending it, I would explain to the patient why I am referring him to a specialist, answer his questions about what to expect, discuss how soon he should be seen given his symptoms, and confirm the best phone number or email for the endodontist's office to reach him.

scenario_text: A radiograph reveals an impacted tooth 3.8 positioned close to the inferior alveolar canal, requiring surgical removal that is beyond your scope. The patient needs to be referred to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon.
task_instruction: Prepare the referral documentation for the oral surgeon.
competent_behaviors: Explains to the patient the reason for referring to a surgical specialist
Discusses the general nature of the procedure and possible risks at a basic level
Answers the patient's questions about next steps
Confirms the patient consents to being referred

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Includes the patient's identifying details and clearly states tooth 3.8 as the tooth of concern
Describes the impaction and its relevant anatomic proximity to the inferior alveolar canal
Attaches or references the radiograph demonstrating the impaction and canal proximity
States the reason for referral, surgical extraction beyond the scope of general practice given the anatomic risk
Includes relevant medical history or medications the surgeon should be aware of before the consultation

critical_errors: Omits the anatomic concern about proximity to the inferior alveolar canal entirely from the referral
Refers the wrong tooth number
Fails to include any radiograph or description allowing the surgeon to assess the case before the patient arrives
model_answer: The referral would state: 'Referral to Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery. Patient: [name, date of birth, contact information]. Tooth 3.8, impacted, mesioangular position. Radiograph enclosed demonstrating close proximity of the roots to the inferior alveolar canal. Reason for referral: surgical extraction with anatomic risk to the inferior alveolar nerve, beyond the scope of general practice. Relevant medical history: [list any conditions or medications]. Please assess and advise regarding surgical plan and any nerve-related risks to discuss with the patient.' I would explain to the patient why this requires a surgical specialist, describe in general terms what the procedure and consultation will involve, mention that there is a nerve located near the tooth that needs careful assessment, answer his questions, and confirm he is comfortable being referred before sending the paperwork.

scenario_text: A patient is missing teeth 3.6, 3.7, 4.6, and 4.7, a bilateral distal extension situation in the mandibular arch (Kennedy Class I). Remaining teeth and periodontal support are healthy. The patient has agreed to a removable partial denture (RPD).
task_instruction: Describe the removable partial denture design you would prescribe for this arch.
competent_behaviors: Explains the general concept of the design to the patient in plain language
Discusses expected function and limitations of a distal extension RPD
Answers the patient's questions about care and maintenance of the appliance
Discusses realistic expectations for chewing efficiency and adjustment period

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Correctly identifies the classification as Kennedy Class I, bilateral distal extension
Specifies an appropriate major connector for the mandibular arch, such as a lingual bar, given adequate vestibular depth and no lingual tori
Specifies direct retainers appropriate for a distal extension case, such as I-bar or circumferential clasps with mesial rests on the most posterior abutments, teeth 3.5 and 4.5
Specifies indirect retention to resist rotation around the fulcrum line, such as rests placed on the mesial aspect of anterior teeth
Specifies denture base extension to cover the full distal extension ridge areas for support

critical_errors: Prescribes a design that is not appropriate for a bilateral distal extension case, such as omitting indirect retention entirely with no rationale
Fails to specify any major connector or retainer design at all
Fails to discuss the design with the patient or obtain his understanding before proceeding to impressions
model_answer: This is a Kennedy Class I, bilateral distal extension situation. I would design a lingual bar major connector, since there is adequate vestibular depth and no interfering lingual tori, connecting the two sides of the arch. For direct retention, I would place mesial occlusal rests on the most posterior remaining abutment teeth, 3.5 and 4.5, with retentive clasp arms engaging the mesiobuccal undercut of those teeth, using an RPI or I-bar style clasp assembly to minimize torque on the abutments during ridge tissue displacement. For indirect retention, I would place small rests on the mesial marginal ridges of the anterior teeth, or on the most anterior remaining premolars, to resist rotation of the denture base around the fulcrum line formed by the direct retainers. The denture base would extend to cover the full extent of both retromolar pads and the distal extension ridges for maximum support. I would explain to the patient that a distal extension partial relies partly on soft tissue support, so some adjustment period and periodic relining should be expected, and answer any questions he has about cleaning and wearing the appliance.

scenario_text: A patient is missing tooth 1.4. Teeth 1.3 and 1.5 are healthy, well aligned, with adequate crown height and no significant restorations. The patient prefers a fixed solution and does not want a dental implant.
task_instruction: Describe the fixed partial denture (bridge) design you would prescribe.
competent_behaviors: Explains why a three-unit fixed bridge is a reasonable option given the patient's preference
Discusses the need to prepare healthy abutment teeth as a tradeoff of this design
Answers the patient's questions about longevity and maintenance, including cleaning under the pontic
Discusses realistic expectations and alternatives briefly, including the implant option he declined

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Specifies a three-unit fixed partial denture with abutments at teeth 1.3 and 1.5 and a pontic replacing 1.4
Specifies an appropriate pontic design for the area, such as an ovate or modified ridge lap pontic for good esthetics and hygiene access
Specifies full coverage retainers on 1.3 and 1.5 appropriate for the material chosen, such as all ceramic given the esthetic zone
Notes the need for adequate connector height and width between units for strength
Recommends floss threaders or a similar aid for cleaning beneath the pontic to maintain periodontal health

critical_errors: Proposes preparing a tooth that is not an abutment, or omits an abutment tooth entirely from the design
Fails to specify a pontic at all for the edentulous space
Fails to discuss the tradeoff of preparing healthy abutment teeth with the patient before proceeding
model_answer: Given the patient's preference against an implant, I would design a three-unit fixed partial denture using teeth 1.3 and 1.5 as abutments and a pontic replacing tooth 1.4. Since this is in the esthetic zone, I would choose an all-ceramic material for both retainers and the pontic, with an ovate pontic design that seats into a small prepared soft tissue concavity for a natural emergence profile and easier hygiene access. The connectors between the pontic and each retainer would need adequate height and width to resist fracture under function. I would explain to the patient that this requires preparing two healthy teeth, 1.3 and 1.5, for crowns, which is a tradeoff compared to an implant that would not involve those teeth, and I would confirm he understands and accepts this before proceeding. I would also show him how to use a floss threader or interdental brush to clean under the pontic daily to protect the gum tissue and abutment teeth long term.

scenario_text: You have prepared tooth 1.6 for a full coverage crown following root canal treatment. The tooth has adequate remaining structure and the patient wants a durable, natural-looking result. You need to send a prescription to the dental laboratory.
task_instruction: Write the laboratory prescription for the crown.
competent_behaviors: Explains to the patient what type of crown is being ordered and why
Answers the patient's questions about appearance and durability
Confirms the expected timeline for the crown to be ready with the patient
Documents the prescription details in the patient chart

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Includes patient identification, tooth number 1.6, and the date of the impression
Specifies the material, such as a monolithic or layered zirconia crown appropriate for a posterior tooth requiring strength
Specifies the shade using a recognized shade guide reference taken from the adjacent teeth
Specifies the margin design and location consistent with the preparation, such as a chamfer margin at the prepared finish line
Specifies the requested delivery or turnaround date and the method of impression or digital scan provided

critical_errors: Submits a prescription with the wrong tooth number
Omits the material specification entirely, leaving the laboratory to guess
Fails to include a shade specification when the crown is for a visible or functionally important tooth without any stated rationale
model_answer: The laboratory prescription would read: 'Patient: [name, date of birth]. Tooth 1.6. Impression/scan date: [date]. Restoration: full coverage crown, posterior. Material: monolithic zirconia for strength given the posterior location and history of root canal treatment. Shade: A2 per shade guide, taken from adjacent tooth 1.7. Margin design: chamfer finish line as prepared, supragingival on the buccal. Occlusion: adjust to light contact in maximum intercuspation and function, avoid contacts in excursive movements creating interference. Requested delivery date: [date, approximately two weeks].' I would explain to the patient that we are ordering a strong ceramic crown matched to his natural tooth colour, answer any questions he has about how it will look and how long it should last, and let him know when to expect his crown seating appointment.

scenario_text: You have completed final impressions for a maxillary removable partial denture replacing teeth 1.4, 1.5, 2.4, and 2.5 in a patient with healthy remaining teeth. You need to send the case to the laboratory for fabrication of the metal framework and denture teeth.
task_instruction: Write the laboratory prescription for the removable partial denture.
competent_behaviors: Explains to the patient the steps remaining before the appliance is delivered
Answers the patient's questions about the try-in appointment
Confirms realistic expectations about the timeline
Documents the prescription in the chart

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Includes patient identification and clearly lists the teeth being replaced, 1.4, 1.5, 2.4, and 2.5
Specifies the framework material, such as a cobalt chromium alloy framework
Specifies the clasp and rest design and locations consistent with the design already discussed with the patient
Specifies the denture tooth shade and mould appropriate to match the adjacent natural teeth
Requests a metal framework try-in stage before final tooth set-up and processing

critical_errors: Submits a prescription listing the wrong teeth to be replaced
Omits the framework material entirely
Skips the try-in stage request without any clinical justification, risking an unverified fit
model_answer: The laboratory prescription would read: 'Patient: [name, date of birth]. Maxillary removable partial denture replacing teeth 1.4, 1.5, 2.4, and 2.5. Framework material: cobalt chromium alloy. Major connector: [as designed, for example a palatal strap]. Clasps and rests: circumferential clasps with mesial and distal rests on abutment teeth as marked on the enclosed design drawing and cast. Denture teeth: shade A2, mould to match existing anterior tooth form. Please fabricate metal framework and return for clinical try-in prior to tooth set-up and final processing.' I would explain to the patient that the next step is trying in the metal framework to check fit before the teeth are set and the appliance is finished, answer any questions about how many appointments remain, and give him a realistic sense of the overall timeline.

scenario_text: Tooth 4.6 has a large carious lesion involving the pulp with a poor long-term prognosis for restoration even with root canal treatment, due to extensive loss of tooth structure and a vertical crack noted on the distal marginal ridge. Extraction with implant or bridge replacement is also reasonable.
task_instruction: Discuss the treatment options with the patient.
competent_behaviors: Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions throughout
Discusses the patient's own priorities and concerns about each option
Discusses fees at a general level for each option
Checks whether the patient has any special circumstances relevant to the decision

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Summarizes the clinical problem with tooth 4.6 in plain language, including the poor long-term prognosis
Presents more than one complete treatment option, such as root canal treatment and crown versus extraction with replacement
Explains the advantages and disadvantages of each option, including the guarded prognosis of attempting to save the tooth given the crack
States a recommended or preferred option based on clinical findings
Verifies the patient understands the explanation before moving forward

critical_errors: Presents only one option as though no alternative exists
Fails to disclose the guarded prognosis and crack, allowing the patient to believe the tooth can be reliably saved
Proceeds to schedule treatment without confirming the patient understands and agrees with the plan
model_answer: I would explain to the patient that tooth 4.6 has a deep cavity that has reached the nerve, and that there is also a crack running down into the tooth from the chewing surface, which significantly worsens the long-term outlook even with root canal treatment and a crown. I would present two complete options: attempting to save the tooth with root canal treatment and a crown, understanding the prognosis is guarded because of the crack, or extracting the tooth and replacing the space, for example with an implant or a bridge. I would explain that saving the tooth avoids extraction now but carries a real risk of the crack progressing and the tooth eventually needing extraction anyway, while extraction is more definitive but requires a healing period and a separate replacement decision. I would give a general sense of the fees involved for each path, note that I would recommend extraction and replacement given the poor prognosis, ask whether he has any particular concerns or circumstances that matter to his decision, and check that he understood everything before we choose a plan together.

scenario_text: A patient with generally healthy teeth asks about options to whiten his smile before an upcoming wedding in six weeks. He has some mild sensitivity to cold and two visible composite restorations on his upper front teeth, 1.1 and 2.1.
task_instruction: Discuss cosmetic whitening options with the patient.
competent_behaviors: Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses fees at a general level for the options presented
Discusses the patient's timeline and priorities for the wedding
Checks whether he has any other concerns about his smile

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Summarizes the relevant clinical findings, including mild sensitivity and existing visible restorations on 1.1 and 2.1
Presents more than one complete option, such as in-office whitening and take-home custom tray whitening
Explains the advantages and disadvantages of each option, including expected sensitivity and timeline to results
Explains that existing composite restorations will not change shade and may need replacement after whitening to match
Verifies the patient understands before proceeding with a chosen option

critical_errors: Fails to mention that the existing visible restorations will not whiten and may look mismatched afterward
Recommends a whitening approach without any consideration of his reported sensitivity
Presents whitening as guaranteed to be completed and stable well before the wedding without any realistic caveat
model_answer: I would explain that he has a couple of good options: in-office whitening, which gives faster results in one or two visits, or take-home custom trays with a professional gel, which take a bit longer but can be gentler and allow him to control the level of whitening. I would explain that either option can cause some temporary increased sensitivity, which is worth knowing given he already reports mild cold sensitivity, and that we would use a desensitizing approach to manage this. I would specifically point out that his composite restorations on 1.1 and 2.1 will not change colour with whitening, so once his natural teeth lighten, those fillings may look slightly darker or mismatched, and he may want to consider replacing them afterward to match the new shade. Given his six week timeline, I would recommend starting soon to allow time for results and any touch ups. I would discuss the approximate cost of each option, ask about any other concerns with his smile, answer his questions, and confirm which option he would like to proceed with.

scenario_text: Radiographs show an impacted tooth 1.8 causing recurrent pericoronitis. You have determined surgical extraction is indicated and will perform it yourself, as it is within your scope. The patient has never had a tooth extracted before and appears anxious.
task_instruction: Obtain informed consent from the patient for the extraction.
competent_behaviors: Acknowledges the patient's anxiety and reassures him appropriately
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions before signing
Discusses fees associated with the procedure
Discusses what to expect on the day of the procedure in general terms

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains the diagnosis and the reason extraction is recommended, recurrent pericoronitis from the impacted tooth
Explains the nature of the procedure itself in understandable terms

Discloses material risks specific to this extraction, such as pain, swelling, bleeding, infection, and the risk of oroantral communication or sinus perforation given the tooth's proximity to the maxillary sinus
Discusses reasonable alternatives, including no treatment and the associated risks of continued pericoronitis
Verifies the patient understands the information and voluntarily agrees before obtaining signed consent

critical_errors: Obtains a signature on a consent form without any verbal explanation of the procedure or risks
Fails to disclose any material risk relevant to this specific extraction
Proceeds to treatment despite clear signs the patient does not understand or has not actually agreed
model_answer: I would start by acknowledging that many people feel anxious about their first extraction and reassure him that we will go step by step and manage his comfort throughout. I would explain that tooth 1.8 is impacted and has been causing repeated infections around the gum tissue, which is why I am recommending it be removed. I would describe the procedure in plain terms, numbing the area, loosening and removing the tooth, and possibly placing a stitch. I would disclose the material risks, including pain, swelling, bruising, bleeding, infection, dry socket, and the possibility of an oroantral communication or sinus perforation given how close this upper tooth sits to the maxillary sinus, and explain these are uncommon but important to know. I would discuss the alternative of not treating the tooth and the risk of ongoing or worsening pericoronitis, and answer any questions he has, including what to expect on the day itself. Once I am confident he understands and is choosing this voluntarily, I would have him sign the consent form and give him a written copy along with a general estimate of the fee.

scenario_text: A 6 year old child needs a pulpotomy and stainless steel crown on a symptomatic primary tooth 8.4. The child is present with his mother, who will make the treatment decision on his behalf.
task_instruction: Obtain informed consent from the parent for the child's treatment.
competent_behaviors: Speaks to the child at an age-appropriate level to help him feel included
Gives the mother the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses fees associated with the procedure
Reassures the mother about behaviour management strategies that will be used

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains the diagnosis and reason for recommending a pulpotomy and stainless steel crown on tooth 8.4
Explains the procedure itself in terms the mother can understand
Discloses material risks, such as failure of the pulpotomy requiring extraction, infection, or need for future treatment
Discusses reasonable alternatives, including extraction with space maintenance or, less appropriately, no treatment and its risks
Confirms the mother, as the legal decision maker, understands and voluntarily consents before proceeding

critical_errors: Obtains consent from the child rather than the parent as though the child could legally authorize the treatment
Fails to disclose that the pulpotomy may fail and further treatment, including extraction, could still be needed
Proceeds without confirming the mother actually understands and agrees to the specific procedure planned
model_answer: I would explain to the mother that tooth 8.4 has a deep cavity affecting the nerve of this primary tooth, and that I am recommending a pulpotomy, removing the affected nerve tissue and placing a medicated filling, followed by a stainless steel crown to protect and restore the tooth. I would describe what the appointment will involve, including local anesthesia and behaviour management techniques appropriate for his age, and reassure her about how we support anxious children through the visit. I would disclose the risks, including the possibility the pulpotomy does not succeed and the tooth later needs extraction, as well as risks of infection or discomfort. I would discuss the alternative of extraction with a space maintainer instead of trying to save the tooth, and briefly the option of no treatment and the risk of worsening infection and pain. I would answer her questions, discuss the estimated fee, and confirm she understands and agrees to the plan before proceeding, since as his parent she is the one providing consent on his behalf.

scenario_text: You need your dental assistant to set up the operatory for a Class II composite restoration on tooth 3.6, including specific matrix and shade materials, and to seat the next patient in fifteen minutes.
task_instruction: Communicate the necessary instructions to your dental assistant.
competent_behaviors: Uses a respectful, collaborative tone rather than an abrupt or commanding one
Thanks the assistant for their help
Checks in on the assistant's workload and availability before assigning tasks
Confirms mutual understanding of the timeline

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Clearly states the specific tooth, 3.6, and procedure being prepared for
Specifies the exact materials needed, such as matrix system, composite shade, and any specific instruments
Provides a clear timeline for when the room needs to be ready
Confirms the assistant has the information needed by asking if there are any questions
Checks back or asks for confirmation once the setup is complete before the next patient arrives

critical_errors: Gives instructions so vague that the correct tooth, procedure, or materials cannot reasonably be determined
Communicates in a disrespectful or demeaning manner toward the assistant
Fails to confirm the setup was actually completed before proceeding with the next patient
model_answer: I would say something like, 'When you have a moment, could you set up operatory two for a Class II composite on tooth 3.6? We will need a sectional matrix system, the composite shade kit, and the usual restorative tray. I would like the room ready in about fifteen minutes since that is when our next patient is scheduled. Does that work with what else you have going on right now, and do you have any questions about the setup?' I would use a collaborative tone, checking on their current workload rather than assuming they are free, and thank them for their help. Before the patient arrives, I would briefly check that the room is ready and confirm with the assistant that everything requested is in place, so we can start the appointment on time.

scenario_text: You discover that a dental assistant sterilized a tray of instruments using an incorrect cycle setting, resulting in instruments that may not be properly sterilized. The assistant appears embarrassed and worried about the mistake.
task_instruction: Address this situation with the staff member.
competent_behaviors: Speaks privately rather than in front of other staff or patients
Uses a calm, non-punitive tone
Reassures the assistant that mistakes can be addressed constructively
Thanks the assistant for being forthcoming about the error if applicable

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Confirms the specific instruments affected and removes them from use immediately
Arranges for the affected instruments to be properly resterilized before any patient use
Reviews the correct sterilization protocol with the assistant to prevent recurrence
Documents the incident and the corrective action taken according to office protocol

critical_errors: Allows the improperly sterilized instruments to be used on a patient despite knowing about the error
Publicly humiliates or berates the staff member in front of colleagues or patients
Fails to take any corrective action or document the incident at all
model_answer: I would first pull the assistant aside privately, away from other staff and patients, and calmly explain what I noticed about the sterilization cycle. I would reassure them that the priority right now is fixing the issue safely, not assigning blame, since mistakes happen and what matters is how we respond. I would immediately confirm which instruments were affected, remove them from circulation, and arrange for them to go through a proper sterilization cycle before they are used on any patient. I would then review the correct cycle settings and protocol together with the assistant to make sure the process is clear going forward, and thank them for letting me know or for cooperating in identifying the affected tray. Finally, I would document what happened and the corrective steps taken, following our office's incident reporting protocol, to maintain a clear record and support quality improvement.

scenario_text: You have just completed a surgical extraction of impacted tooth 3.8 on an adult patient. The patient is ready to leave the clinic.
task_instruction: Give the patient post-operative instructions before he leaves.
competent_behaviors: Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Provides written instructions in addition to verbal explanation
Confirms the patient has someone to accompany him home if sedation was used
Provides contact information for after-hours concerns

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Instructs the patient to bite on gauze with firm pressure for a specified period to control bleeding
Instructs the patient to avoid rinsing, spitting forcefully, drinking through a straw, or smoking for at least 24 hours to protect the clot
Instructs on appropriate pain management, including recommended medication and dosing
Instructs on diet, such as soft foods and avoiding hot or hard foods for the first day or two
Explains warning signs that should prompt him to contact the office, such as excessive bleeding, fever, or worsening swelling and pain after several days

critical_errors: Fails to warn the patient against activities that dislodge the clot, such as straw use or vigorous rinsing, contributing to a foreseeable dry socket
Provides no guidance at all on managing bleeding or pain after the procedure
Fails to give the patient any way to reach the office if a complication arises
model_answer: I would explain to him that he should bite firmly on the gauze pad for about 30 to 45 minutes to help a clot form, and to replace it with a fresh piece if bleeding continues. I would tell him to avoid rinsing, spitting forcefully, using a straw, or smoking for at least 24 hours, since these can dislodge the clot and lead to a painful dry socket. For pain, I would recommend an over-the-counter anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen at a specific dose, or a prescribed medication if needed, and advise taking it before the anesthetic fully wears off. I would advise a soft, cool diet for the first day or two, avoiding hot liquids and hard or crunchy foods near the extraction site. I would explain that some swelling and mild discomfort are normal for a couple of days, but that he should call the office if he has heavy bleeding that does not stop with pressure, fever, or pain and swelling that worsens after the third day instead of improving. I would give him these instructions in writing as well, provide our after-hours contact number, and ask if he has any questions before leaving.

scenario_text: You have just prepared tooth 1.6 for a crown and placed a provisional crown while the final restoration is fabricated at the laboratory. The patient is ready to leave.
task_instruction: Give the patient post-operative instructions for the provisional crown before he leaves.
competent_behaviors: Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Provides written instructions in addition to verbal explanation
Reassures the patient about the temporary nature and purpose of the provisional
Confirms the date of the return appointment for the final crown

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Instructs the patient to avoid sticky or chewy foods that could dislodge the provisional crown
Instructs the patient to chew on the opposite side or avoid hard foods on that tooth when possible
Advises careful flossing technique, sliding floss out sideways rather than lifting up, to avoid dislodging the provisional
Explains that mild sensitivity to hot, cold, or pressure is normal but should improve, and how to manage it
Instructs the patient to contact the office promptly if the provisional comes loose, falls off, or breaks before the final crown appointment

critical_errors: Fails to warn the patient about foods or habits that commonly dislodge a provisional crown
Gives no instruction on what to do if the provisional comes off before the final crown is seated
Fails to schedule or confirm the return appointment for cementing the final crown
model_answer: I would explain to him that the crown on tooth 1.6 right now is a temporary one, meant to protect the prepared tooth until his final crown is ready from the laboratory. I would advise him to avoid sticky or chewy foods, such as gum or caramel, that could pull the provisional off, and to try chewing on the opposite side or avoiding hard foods on that tooth when possible. For flossing, I would show him to slide the floss out from the side rather than lifting it straight up through the contact, to reduce the chance of dislodging the temporary. I would let him know some mild sensitivity to hot, cold, or biting pressure is normal with a provisional and should improve, and that over-the-counter pain relief can help if needed. Most importantly, I would tell him to call the office right away if the provisional comes loose, falls off, or breaks, since leaving the prepared tooth uncovered can cause sensitivity or shifting of the teeth. I would confirm his appointment date for the final crown, provide written instructions, and answer any questions before he leaves.

scenario_text: A new patient transfers into your practice with a chart from their previous dentist. The chart contains a medical history form, a panoramic radiograph, and a treatment plan for tooth 3.6, but no periodontal charting, no record of informed consent for any prior procedure, and no note of the patient's stated drug allergy that the patient mentions verbally at check-in.
task_instruction: Review the incomplete chart and identify what is missing, then explain to the patient how you will proceed before treatment begins.
competent_behaviors: Thanks the patient for bringing the previous records
Answers any questions the patient raises
Discusses fees for any additional assessment required

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies that periodontal charting is missing and must be completed
Identifies that informed consent documentation is absent for prior procedures
Notes the verbally stated drug allergy in the chart immediately and confirms it with the patient
Explains that a new comprehensive examination is needed before proceeding with tooth 3.6
Communicates the plan clearly and in an organized manner

critical_errors: Proceeds with treatment on tooth 3.6 without completing a periodontal assessment or confirming the allergy
Fails to document the disclosed drug allergy anywhere in the record
model_answer: I would tell the patient: thank you for bringing your previous records, they are very helpful. I notice a few things are missing from the file that I need to complete before I can safely treat you. First, there is no periodontal charting, so I will need to measure your gum pockets today. Second, I do not see any signed consent forms for the work already done, so going forward I will document consent for anything we do together. Third, you mentioned an allergy just now that is not written anywhere in your chart, I am recording that right now so every member of our team sees it before any medication or material is used. Once I have completed a full exam including the periodontal charting, I will review the proposed plan for tooth 3.6 and confirm whether it is still appropriate. Do you have any questions about that process? I am also happy to discuss the fees for today's assessment before we begin.

scenario_text: You are about to perform a scaling procedure on a returning patient. While reviewing the chart you notice the sterilization log for the ultrasonic scaler tip used on the previous patient was not initialed by the assistant, and the tip is sitting on the tray marked as ready for use.
task_instruction: Identify the infection control protocol lapse and determine how you will correct it before treating the patient.
competent_behaviors: Remains calm and professional in front of the patient
Discusses the delay with the patient if it affects the appointment time
Answers any questions the patient has about safety

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Recognizes the sterilization log gap means the tip's status cannot be verified
Removes the unverified instrument from use rather than assuming it was processed
Obtains a properly logged and verified sterile instrument before proceeding
Documents the incident and notifies the team member responsible so the log is corrected going forward

critical_errors: Uses the unverified scaler tip on the patient
Ignores the missing log entry and proceeds without confirming sterilization status
model_answer: I would stop before touching the tray and set the unverified scaler tip aside, since an unsigned sterilization log means I cannot confirm it was actually processed rather than simply placed on the tray. I would ask my assistant to pull a properly logged and verified sterile tip from storage before continuing. I would briefly explain to the patient that I am confirming an instrument before we begin, which may add a minute or two, and answer any questions they raise. After the appointment, I would document the gap in the log and speak with the assistant so the initialing step is completed consistently going forward, since this protects every future patient as well as this one.

scenario_text: A 28 year old patient with no history of trauma or symptoms requests a full mouth series of radiographs because they had one done at a previous dentist two years ago and want it repeated today for their own records.
task_instruction: Make an evidence-based decision about the radiograph request and discuss it with the patient.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Discusses fees associated with any imaging performed
Reviews the patient's stated reason for wanting the images

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Recognizes that current guidelines base radiograph frequency on individualized risk, not routine repetition
Explains that a full series is not indicated without new clinical findings or elapsed recall interval consistent with the patient's risk category
Proposes an appropriate alternative, such as targeted bitewings or a clinical exam to determine actual need
Explains the rationale of minimizing unnecessary radiation exposure to the patient
Verifies the patient understands the recommendation before proceeding

critical_errors: Takes a full mouth series solely because the patient requested it without clinical justification
model_answer: I would explain to the patient that radiograph frequency is based on their individual risk of disease, not on personal preference or how long ago the last set was taken elsewhere, since ALARA principles mean we avoid unnecessary radiation. I would review their chart and clinical exam findings first. If there is no new symptom, no trauma, and their caries and periodontal risk are low, a full series is not indicated today. I would offer to complete a clinical exam and, if warranted, take only the specific bitewings or periapicals that address any actual finding. I would explain that this protects their health while still giving us the information we need, verify they understand, and discuss any fees before proceeding. If they still want copies of their old images for their own records, I would help them request those from the previous office instead.

scenario_text: Current clinical guidelines recommend extraction of an asymptomatic partially erupted third molar (tooth 3.8) showing early mesioangular impaction and a small area of pericoronitis history. The patient strongly prefers to avoid any surgery and asks you to simply monitor the tooth instead.
task_instruction: Weigh the clinical guideline against the patient's preference and determine how to proceed.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Discusses the patient's specific concerns about surgery
Discusses fees for extraction versus continued monitoring

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Summarizes the clinical findings and why the guideline recommends extraction
Presents monitoring as a valid alternative and explains its risks, such as recurrent pericoronitis or further impaction
Respects patient autonomy and does not pressure the patient into surgery they do not want
Documents the discussion, the guideline recommendation, and the patient's informed decision to monitor
Arranges a defined follow-up interval to reassess the tooth

critical_errors: Extracts the tooth against the patient's clearly stated wishes
Fails to document the patient's informed decision to decline the recommended treatment
