model_answer: I would explain to the patient that tooth 3.8 shows a pattern associated with a higher chance of future pericoronitis or complications, which is why the guideline recommends extraction, but I would also acknowledge that monitoring is a reasonable choice if they understand the risks. I would describe what monitoring involves, including watching for pain, swelling, or repeated infection, and explain that those signs would mean extraction becomes more urgent later. I would not pressure them, since the final decision is theirs to make once informed. I would document in the chart that the guideline-based recommendation was discussed, that the patient chose to monitor, and the reasons given. I would schedule a specific recall interval, such as six months, to reassess the tooth and its surrounding tissue at that time, and answer any remaining questions before they leave.

scenario_text: While reviewing a chart before a recall appointment, you notice that the note from the previous visit incorrectly states composite was placed on tooth 2.4 when the treatment ledger and your own memory confirm the restoration was actually placed on tooth 2.5. The error has already been submitted on an insurance claim.
task_instruction: Correct the documentation error appropriately.
competent_behaviors: Remains transparent about the nature of the error
Answers any questions from staff or the patient if raised
Discusses the situation calmly with the team member who made the entry

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Does not delete or overwrite the original erroneous entry
Adds a clearly dated and signed addendum correcting the tooth number to 2.5
Notifies the insurer or billing coordinator so the submitted claim can be corrected
Documents the reason for the correction in the addendum for a clear audit trail

critical_errors: Deletes or alters the original chart entry to hide that an error occurred
Leaves the incorrect tooth number on the insurance claim without correcting it
model_answer: I would never delete or white out the original entry, since the record must show what was actually written at the time. Instead, I would add a new, clearly dated addendum stating that the entry from the prior visit incorrectly listed tooth 2.4 and that the composite restoration was in fact placed on tooth 2.5, with my initials or signature confirming the correction and a brief note of why it is being made. I would then contact the billing coordinator to correct the submitted insurance claim so it reflects the accurate tooth number, since submitting inaccurate information to a third-party payer is a serious concern even when unintentional. I would speak calmly with the staff member who made the original entry to understand how it happened and prevent recurrence, without assigning blame in front of the patient.

scenario_text: A patient calls asking that a diagnosis of periodontitis be left off their chart summary because they are worried it will affect their life insurance application, even though periodontal charting clearly supports the diagnosis.
task_instruction: Respond to the patient's request while managing the patient record appropriately.
competent_behaviors: Listens empathetically to the patient's financial concern
Answers any questions the patient has about how records are used
Discusses the patient's options for requesting records through proper channels

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains that the chart must accurately reflect clinical findings and cannot be altered to omit a supported diagnosis
Clarifies that accurate record-keeping is both a professional and legal obligation
Offers to discuss with the patient how the diagnosis will be communicated if records are requested by a third party under proper consent
Maintains a respectful, non-judgmental tone throughout the conversation

critical_errors: Agrees to omit or falsify the periodontitis diagnosis from the chart
model_answer: I would tell the patient that I understand their concern about the insurance application, but that the chart has to accurately reflect what the periodontal charting shows, since altering or omitting a supported diagnosis would compromise the accuracy of their health record and is not something I am able to do. I would explain that accurate record-keeping is both a professional obligation and, in many cases, a legal one. I would clarify that records are only released to a third party like an insurer with the patient's own consent, and that we can discuss exactly what will be shared and how at that time. I would keep my tone supportive rather than judgmental, since the patient's worry is understandable even though the request cannot be granted, and I would answer any further questions they have about the process.

scenario_text: You are treating a patient for a routine filling on tooth 1.6. Midway through the procedure your assistant, wearing treatment gloves, adjusts their own mask and then reaches for a sterile cotton roll from the open supply container.
task_instruction: Identify the infection control lapse and address it appropriately during the appointment.
competent_behaviors: Addresses the issue calmly without alarming the patient unnecessarily
Answers any questions the patient raises about the pause
Reassures the patient professionally

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Recognizes that touching the mask with treatment gloves contaminated the gloves
Stops the assistant before the contaminated glove touches the sterile cotton roll or supply container
Has the assistant change gloves before continuing and discards any contaminated supplies that were touched
Documents the infection control error consistent with practice protocol

critical_errors: Allows the contaminated glove to touch the open supply container without correction
Continues the procedure using instruments or supplies that were contaminated
model_answer: I would immediately stop my assistant before their gloved hand reaches the sterile cotton roll container, since adjusting the mask with treatment gloves on has contaminated the glove surface. I would ask them to step back, remove the gloves, perform hand hygiene, and put on a fresh pair before touching anything else in the sterile field. If the glove already made contact with the supply container, I would discard the exposed cotton rolls and treat the container as contaminated rather than risk cross-contamination for the patient. I would explain briefly to the patient that we are taking a short pause to maintain proper infection control, which most patients appreciate rather than find alarming. After the appointment, I would document the lapse per our infection control log so the pattern can be tracked and addressed with the team.

scenario_text: A patient with a documented penicillin allergy is scheduled for extraction of tooth 4.8 and prophylactic antibiotics are being considered. The chart's allergy field says penicillin allergy but the treatment note from the previous visit lists amoxicillin as a prescribed medication with no documented reaction.
task_instruction: Make an evidence-based decision about prescribing and correct the chart discrepancy.
competent_behaviors: Confirms directly with the patient what reaction, if any, occurred with amoxicillin
Answers any questions the patient has about their allergy history
Discusses the treatment plan clearly

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Recognizes the contradiction between the documented allergy and the prior amoxicillin prescription
Clarifies the discrepancy directly with the patient before prescribing anything
Avoids penicillin-class antibiotics unless the allergy is confirmed to be inaccurate or resolved through proper verification
Selects an appropriate alternative antibiotic if one is clinically indicated and the allergy stands
Updates the chart with the clarified and accurate allergy information

critical_errors: Prescribes a penicillin-class antibiotic without resolving the documented allergy discrepancy
Leaves the contradictory allergy information uncorrected in the chart
model_answer: Before prescribing anything, I would ask the patient directly about their history with amoxicillin, since the chart shows a documented penicillin allergy but also an apparent prior amoxicillin prescription with no reaction noted, which is a contradiction I need to resolve rather than assume away. If the patient confirms they did react to amoxicillin, or is unsure, I would treat the penicillin allergy as active and avoid the entire class, selecting an appropriate alternative such as cephalexin, azithromycin, or doxycycline if antibiotics are actually indicated for this extraction, since current guidance no longer recommends clindamycin for this purpose due to its higher rate of adverse reactions. If the patient clarifies that the earlier prescription was tolerated with no reaction and the original allergy notation was itself an error, I would still verify carefully before changing anything, and document exactly what the patient reports either way. I would update the allergy field and add a note explaining the clarification so the next provider does not face the same contradiction.

scenario_text: A patient's chart shows they missed their last three recommended periodontal maintenance appointments over 18 months. They now present with generalized 5 to 7mm pocket depths and ask you to just do a routine cleaning like before rather than the more involved treatment you recommend.
task_instruction: Weigh the clinical guideline against the patient's stated preference and decide how to proceed.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Discusses fees for the recommended treatment versus a routine cleaning
Acknowledges the patient's time constraints or reasons for missed appointments

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains why the current pocket depths no longer support a routine prophylaxis alone
Presents the evidence-based recommendation, such as scaling and root planing, and its rationale
Discusses the risks of continuing with only routine cleaning given the disease progression
Respects the patient's right to decline and documents the discussion and the patient's decision

critical_errors: Performs only a routine cleaning on a patient with active periodontitis without disclosing the clinical risk of doing so
Fails to document the patient's informed decision if they decline the recommended treatment
model_answer: I would explain to the patient that when they were last seen regularly, a routine cleaning was appropriate, but the pocket depths I am measuring today, generally 5 to 7mm, indicate active periodontal disease that a routine cleaning will not adequately address. I would recommend scaling and root planing and explain that untreated, this level of disease risks further attachment and bone loss and eventually tooth loss. I would acknowledge that missed appointments happen for real reasons and avoid making them feel judged. I would discuss the fee difference between the two approaches. If, after understanding the risks, the patient still insists on only a routine cleaning, I would document that the recommendation and its rationale were explained, that the risks of declining were disclosed, and that the patient chose the alternative, since I cannot force treatment but must ensure they are making an informed choice.

scenario_text: You are reviewing charts before your day begins and notice that a patient scheduled for a crown seating on tooth 2.6 this afternoon has no documented consent form on file for the crown preparation performed two weeks ago, though the procedure note describes the appointment in detail.
task_instruction: Identify the missing documentation and address it before proceeding with today's appointment.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient has when discussing consent
Discusses the patient's understanding of the procedure already completed
Explains today's seating appointment clearly

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Recognizes that a signed consent form is missing for the prior crown preparation
Discusses the prior procedure with the patient today to confirm they understood and agreed to it at the time
Obtains and documents retrospective acknowledgment or, at minimum, clearly notes the gap and the steps taken
Ensures proper informed consent is obtained and documented before proceeding with today's crown seating

critical_errors: Proceeds with the crown seating without any consent documentation for either the prior or the current procedure
Fabricates a consent record to appear as though it was completed at the time of the original procedure
model_answer: Before this afternoon's appointment, I would flag that no signed consent form exists for the crown preparation performed two weeks ago, even though the clinical note documents the procedure. I would not fabricate a form to make it look like consent was obtained at the time, since that would misrepresent the record. Instead, when the patient arrives, I would discuss the prior procedure with them, confirm they understood what was done and agreed to it, and document that conversation clearly with today's date, noting it addresses a documentation gap from the prior visit. For today's crown seating itself, I would ensure proper informed consent is discussed and documented before proceeding, including the risks, benefits, and alternatives of seating the permanent crown, so this appointment does not repeat the same gap.

scenario_text: A locum dentist covering your practice for two weeks left several patient charts with treatment notes but no corresponding entries in the digital scheduling and billing system, so procedures performed on teeth 1.4, 1.5, and 3.7 for three different patients cannot be reconciled with what was billed.
task_instruction: Address the record-keeping gap left by the locum before continuing patient care.
competent_behaviors: Approaches the situation without placing blame on staff in front of patients
Answers any questions from the practice manager or team
Discusses next steps calmly with the office team

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Cross-references the paper or digital treatment notes against the billing system for each affected patient
Corrects or completes any missing digital entries to match the actual documented treatment
Verifies that billed procedures match what was actually documented and performed for each patient
Contacts the locum dentist if clarification is needed on any ambiguous note
Documents the reconciliation process and any corrections made

critical_errors: Leaves the discrepancy unresolved and allows inaccurate billing to stand
Fabricates missing details rather than verifying them against the actual treatment notes or contacting the locum for clarification
model_answer: I would pull each of the three affected charts and compare the locum's treatment notes for teeth 1.4, 1.5, and 3.7 against what was actually entered into the scheduling and billing system, looking for any mismatch. Where the digital record is simply missing an entry that matches the treatment note, I would complete it accurately based on the documented procedure. Where a note is ambiguous or I cannot confirm exactly what was billed versus performed, I would contact the locum dentist directly to clarify before making any changes, rather than guessing. I would verify that the final billing accurately reflects the procedures actually performed for each patient. Throughout this, I would keep the conversation with my team professional and solution-focused rather than blaming anyone, and I would document the steps taken to reconcile the records so there is a clear trail of the correction.

scenario_text: Current evidence-based guidelines recommend a single specific preoperative dose of amoxicillin for infective endocarditis prophylaxis in a patient with a prosthetic heart valve before extraction of tooth 1.8. A colleague in your office suggests giving half that dose, saying it has always worked for their patients.
task_instruction: Make an evidence-based prescribing decision for this patient.
competent_behaviors: Discusses the difference of opinion with the colleague respectfully
Answers any questions the patient has about the antibiotic regimen
Confirms the patient's allergy history before prescribing

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Recognizes that current evidence-based guidelines specify a single, particular preoperative dose for infective endocarditis prophylaxis, not a multi-day course
Declines to substitute a colleague's personal preference for a reduced dose without clinical justification
Prescribes the full guideline-recommended single dose, timed appropriately before the procedure, for this patient's specific risk category
Documents the rationale for following the guideline-based dose in the chart

critical_errors: Prescribes the colleague's reduced dose instead of the evidence-based guideline dose for a patient with a prosthetic heart valve
Fails to verify the patient's allergy status before prescribing prophylactic antibiotics
model_answer: I would thank my colleague for sharing their experience but explain that for a patient with a prosthetic heart valve, infective endocarditis prophylaxis needs to follow the current evidence-based guideline for the single preoperative dose, since anecdotal success with a reduced dose in other patients does not substitute for the established recommendation in a high-risk case like this, and this is a single dose given before the procedure rather than a multi-day course. I would confirm the patient has no allergy to amoxicillin before prescribing. I would prescribe the full guideline-recommended dose exactly as specified, timed appropriately before the extraction, rather than the reduced amount my colleague suggested. I would document in the chart that the prophylaxis followed the current evidence-based protocol given the patient's prosthetic valve, so the reasoning is clear to anyone reviewing the record later. I would also answer any questions the patient has about why the antibiotic is necessary and how to take it correctly.

scenario_text: You discover that a chart audit template used in your office has patients' full health histories, including HIV status where noted, visible on a shared computer screen in the reception area whenever any staff member opens a chart to check a patient in.
task_instruction: Address the privacy and record management issue you have identified.
competent_behaviors: Raises the concern professionally with the practice manager or owner
Answers any questions from staff about the change
Discusses the importance of patient trust with the team

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Recognizes that displaying sensitive health information on a screen visible to others in reception is a privacy breach risk
Proposes a practical fix such as a check-in view that shows only scheduling information, not full health history
Ensures screens are repositioned or privacy filters are used so sensitive information is not visible to others
Documents or communicates the policy change to the whole team so it is applied consistently

critical_errors: Takes no action despite recognizing the ongoing privacy exposure
Continues to display full sensitive health information at the check-in screen after identifying the issue
model_answer: I would recognize immediately that having full health histories, including something as sensitive as HIV status, visible on a screen anyone in the waiting area could glimpse is a real privacy risk and needs to change right away, not just get flagged for later. I would raise it with the practice manager and propose a practical solution, such as configuring the check-in screen to show only scheduling details like name and appointment time rather than clinical history, with full charts only accessible from a separate screen not facing the reception area. I would suggest repositioning monitors or adding privacy filters as an immediate interim step while the software view is adjusted. I would communicate the change to the whole team so everyone understands why it matters and applies it consistently, and I would answer any questions staff have about protecting patient confidentiality going forward.

scenario_text: A patient presents for a scheduled restoration on tooth 2.7 but their chart's medical history update form, due to be refreshed annually, was last completed 14 months ago. The front desk checked the patient in without flagging the overdue update.
task_instruction: Address the outdated record before proceeding with treatment.
competent_behaviors: Explains to the patient why an updated history is needed
Answers any questions the patient raises
Thanks the patient for their patience with the additional step

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Recognizes that the medical history is overdue for its annual update before treatment proceeds
Has the patient complete an updated medical history form or verbally reviews and updates it before treatment
Confirms there have been no new diagnoses, medications, or allergies since the last update
Documents the updated history in the chart with the current date before proceeding

critical_errors: Proceeds with the restoration without updating the overdue medical history
Assumes no changes have occurred without confirming with the patient
model_answer: Before starting the restoration on tooth 2.7, I would notice that the medical history on file is 14 months old and overdue for its annual update, so I would pause and have the patient complete an updated history form, or review it verbally with them if that is faster, before any treatment begins. I would specifically ask whether there have been any new diagnoses, new medications, or new allergies since the last update, since any of those could change how I safely proceed. I would document the updated history with today's date in the chart. I would explain to the patient briefly why this extra step matters, thank them for their patience, and answer any questions they have, and I would also mention to the front desk afterward that overdue history updates should be flagged at check-in going forward.

scenario_text: A patient asks you to backdate a treatment note for a filling on tooth 4.5 so that it falls within their current insurance benefit year, even though the procedure will actually be performed next week, after the benefit year has already ended.
task_instruction: Respond to the patient's request regarding the treatment record.
competent_behaviors: Listens to the patient's financial concern with empathy
Answers any questions the patient has about their coverage
Discusses alternative ways to manage the cost

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Declines to backdate the treatment note, explaining that records must reflect the actual date of service
Explains that backdating would constitute insurance fraud and expose both the patient and the practice to serious consequences
Offers a legitimate alternative, such as checking if the procedure can genuinely be completed before the benefit year ends, or discussing a payment plan
Maintains a respectful, non-judgmental tone while being clear about the record-keeping requirement

critical_errors: Agrees to backdate the treatment note to misrepresent the actual date of service
model_answer: I would tell the patient that I understand the frustration of losing insurance coverage right before a procedure, but that I am not able to backdate the treatment note, since the record has to reflect the actual date the filling on tooth 4.5 is performed. I would explain that submitting a record with an inaccurate date to an insurer would be considered fraud, which carries serious consequences for both of us, so it is not something I can do regardless of the circumstances. I would look instead at whether the appointment could genuinely be moved earlier if there is any remaining time in the benefit year, and if not, I would discuss options like a payment plan or phased treatment to help manage the cost. I would keep my tone understanding rather than judgmental throughout, since the patient's concern about cost is legitimate even though the specific request cannot be granted.

scenario_text: Your practice recently switched to a new electronic charting system. While reviewing your schedule you notice that a periodontal maintenance recall for a patient with a history of aggressive periodontitis was never migrated from the old system and the patient has gone 20 months without a recall visit as a result.
task_instruction: Address the gap in the patient's recall record and follow-up care.
competent_behaviors: Contacts the patient promptly and courteously
Answers any questions the patient has about the gap
Apologizes appropriately for the administrative error without being defensive

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies that the recall was lost during the system migration rather than assuming the patient simply did not book
Contacts the patient directly to schedule an overdue periodontal maintenance appointment as soon as possible
Reviews the migration process to identify whether other patients with a similar history may have been missed
Documents the gap and the corrective action taken in the patient's chart
Puts a safeguard in place, such as a manual cross-check, to prevent recurrence during any future system changes

critical_errors: Fails to contact the patient or arrange a follow-up appointment after identifying the missed recall
Does not check whether other patients were similarly affected by the same migration error
model_answer: I would contact the patient directly and courteously to explain that a data migration error meant their periodontal maintenance recall did not carry over to our new system, and apologize for the gap without being defensive about it, since the patient's care was affected regardless of the cause. I would schedule them for an overdue maintenance appointment as soon as reasonably possible given their history of aggressive periodontitis. I would then review the migration to see if other patients with similar recall needs were also missed, since this is likely a systemic issue rather than a one-off. I would document the gap, the outreach, and the new appointment in the chart, and put a safeguard in place, such as a manual audit of high-risk recall patients after any future system change, so this does not happen again.

scenario_text: You are treating an anxious patient for a Class II composite restoration on tooth 4.6. Midway through, you realize you forgot to place a rubber dam, which is your usual protocol and the standard indicated in the treatment note you already wrote before starting.
task_instruction: Address the deviation between what was documented and what was actually done.
competent_behaviors: Explains to the patient calmly if isolation needs to be adjusted mid-procedure
Answers any questions the patient has
Manages the anxious patient's comfort throughout

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Recognizes the discrepancy between the pre-written treatment note and the actual isolation method used
Takes clinically appropriate action, such as placing isolation now if still feasible and beneficial, rather than ignoring the gap
Corrects the treatment note to accurately reflect what isolation method was actually used, rather than leaving inaccurate documentation
Reflects on the workflow habit of pre-writing notes before treatment is complete to prevent recurrence

critical_errors: Leaves the treatment note stating a rubber dam was placed when it was not, without correcting it
Continues the composite restoration without addressing moisture control at all despite recognizing the omission
model_answer: Once I realize the rubber dam was never placed even though my note already says it was, I would first address the clinical issue: if we are still early enough in the procedure that isolation would meaningfully improve the outcome, I would place it now, explaining calmly to the anxious patient why we are pausing briefly. If it is genuinely too late in the procedure to add it without compromising what has already been done, I would use the best available alternative isolation method for the remainder. Regardless of what I do clinically, I would correct the treatment note before it is finalized so it accurately reflects the isolation method actually used, since documenting a rubber dam that was not placed would misrepresent the record. I would also make a personal note to stop pre-writing procedure notes before treatment is actually complete, since that habit created this discrepancy in the first place.

scenario_text: Current evidence-based guidance suggests fluoride varnish application at recall visits for a patient with high caries risk, but the patient tells you they read online that fluoride is unnecessary and possibly harmful, and they would prefer you skip it at every visit going forward.
task_instruction: Weigh the clinical guideline against the patient's stated preference and respond appropriately.
competent_behaviors: Listens respectfully to the patient's concern without dismissing it
Answers any questions the patient has about fluoride safety
Discusses the source of the patient's information calmly

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains the evidence supporting fluoride varnish for a high caries risk patient
Addresses the specific safety concern the patient raises with accurate information
Respects the patient's right to decline after being informed and does not apply the varnish against their wishes
Documents the discussion and the patient's informed decision in the chart

critical_errors: Applies fluoride varnish despite the patient's clear refusal after being informed
Dismisses the patient's concern without providing any accurate information to address it
model_answer: I would listen to the patient's concern without dismissing it, and ask what specifically they read so I can address it directly. I would explain that for someone at high caries risk like them, fluoride varnish applied at recall visits is supported by strong evidence for reducing new decay, and that at the concentrations and frequency used in a dental office, it has a well-established safety profile, addressing the specific safety worry they raised as accurately as I can. I would answer any follow-up questions. If, after hearing this, the patient still prefers to decline fluoride varnish going forward, I would respect that decision, since it is ultimately theirs to make once properly informed, and I would not apply it against their wishes. I would document that the evidence-based recommendation was discussed, the patient's specific concern was addressed, and the patient chose to decline.

scenario_text: During a busy afternoon, you notice a colleague performing an extraction on tooth 3.5 has not documented the local anesthetic type, dose, or injection site anywhere in the chart, even though the procedure is now complete and the patient has left the operatory.
task_instruction: Address the missing documentation you have observed.
competent_behaviors: Raises the issue with the colleague privately rather than in front of other staff or patients
Answers any questions the colleague has about the concern
Discusses the importance of complete records without being accusatory

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies that anesthetic type, dose, and injection site are missing from the chart for a completed procedure
Brings the gap to the colleague's attention promptly so it can be completed while still fresh in memory
Encourages the colleague to document the missing details as a contemporaneous addendum rather than leaving it blank
Reinforces the importance of complete anesthetic documentation for patient safety and legal accuracy

critical_errors: Ignores the missing anesthetic documentation entirely
Suggests documenting an anesthetic type, dose, or site the colleague cannot actually confirm was used
model_answer: I would speak with my colleague privately, away from other staff and patients, and mention that I noticed the chart for the extraction on tooth 3.5 does not yet include the anesthetic type, dose, or injection site. I would frame it as a helpful reminder rather than a criticism, since documentation gaps happen on busy days. I would encourage them to complete the entry now, while the details are still fresh, as a contemporaneous note rather than leaving it blank or filling it in inaccurately later from memory alone. I would emphasize that this information matters both for patient safety, in case of any reaction or complication later, and for the legal completeness of the record. I would answer any questions they have and keep the conversation supportive rather than accusatory.

scenario_text: A patient with a documented latex allergy is scheduled for a restoration on tooth 1.5. Your clinic's standard supply cart includes latex dam material and latex-containing gloves as the default stock, and no alternate cart has been prepared for this appointment.
task_instruction: Ensure the appropriate protocol is followed given the patient's documented allergy before treatment begins.
competent_behaviors: Confirms the allergy directly with the patient before starting
Answers any questions the patient has about the precautions being taken
Reassures the patient calmly about the steps being taken for their safety

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Reviews the chart and confirms the documented latex allergy before setting up for the appointment
Ensures all latex-containing materials, including gloves and dam material, are removed from the treatment area
Substitutes latex-free gloves, dam material, and any other latex-containing supplies before the patient enters the operatory
Documents that latex-free protocol was followed for this appointment

critical_errors: Uses latex gloves or latex dam material on a patient with a documented latex allergy
Proceeds with treatment without verifying and preparing the operatory for the allergy beforehand
model_answer: Before this patient even enters the operatory, I would review the chart, confirm the documented latex allergy, and prepare a latex-free setup, since the standard supply cart contains latex gloves and latex dam material by default and I cannot rely on that cart for this appointment. I would have the team remove or replace every latex-containing item in the treatment area, including gloves, dam material, and any other supplies that might contain latex, with confirmed latex-free alternatives. When the patient arrives, I would confirm the allergy with them directly as an extra safety check, and explain the precautions we have taken so they feel confident nothing in the room will trigger a reaction. I would document in the chart that a latex-free protocol was followed for this visit, so the precaution is clearly recorded alongside the allergy itself.

scenario_text: A 34-year-old patient attends for a recall examination. Charting and radiographs show three new interproximal carious lesions since the last visit two years ago, a dry mouth from a new blood pressure medication, and frequent between-meal sugary coffee drinks reported in the history.
task_instruction: Discuss the patient's caries risk with them and outline a prevention plan.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances if applicable
Discusses fees for any recommended products or services

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies the patient as high caries risk and explains why (new lesions, xerostomia, frequent sugar exposure)
Explains the link between the new medication, reduced salivary flow, and increased caries risk
Recommends a specific modifiable behaviour change (reducing frequency of sugary drinks, using xylitol gum or saliva substitute)
Recommends an appropriate preventive measure (prescription-strength fluoride toothpaste or in-office fluoride varnish)
Verifies the patient understands the plan and communicates in an organized, non-judgemental manner

critical_errors: Blames or shames the patient for the new lesions without discussing contributing factors
Fails to mention the medication-related dry mouth despite it being clearly documented in the history
model_answer: I want to talk with you about why we are seeing three new spots of decay since your last visit. Looking at your chart, a few things are working against your teeth right now. First, your new blood pressure medication can reduce how much saliva you make, and saliva is what naturally rinses sugar and acid off your teeth and helps repair early decay. Second, you mentioned sipping sugary coffee drinks throughout the day, and every sip resets an acid attack on your enamel, so frequency matters more than the total amount. Based on this I would classify you as higher risk for new cavities right now, not because of anything you did wrong, but because of how these factors are combining. Here is what I recommend. Try to limit the sugary coffee drinks to mealtimes rather than sipping all day, and rinse with plain water in between if you do have one. I would also like to prescribe a higher-concentration fluoride toothpaste for you to use at night, and we can apply a fluoride varnish here today to help remineralize the early lesions. If your mouth continues to feel dry, a saliva substitute or sugar-free xylitol gum can help stimulate flow. Does this plan make sense to you, and do you have any questions about the medication or the products I mentioned? We can also go over the cost of the varnish and the prescription toothpaste before you leave today.

scenario_text: A single parent brings in a 7-year-old for an emergency visit for pain on tooth 8.4. The parent explains they have missed several recommended cleanings because they cannot afford transportation to the clinic and work two jobs with limited time off.
task_instruction: Discuss the socioeconomic barriers to care with the parent and identify realistic options to improve the child's access to dental care.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the parent raises
Gives the parent the opportunity to ask questions
Acknowledges the parent's circumstances without judgement
Discusses fees and payment options for today's visit

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Acknowledges the transportation and time barriers described without minimizing them
Asks whether the family is aware of or enrolled in a public dental benefit program for children
Suggests practical scheduling solutions such as early morning, combined sibling appointments, or a fixed recall reminder system
Verifies the parent understands the plan and feels it is realistic for their situation

critical_errors: Dismisses the parent's stated barriers as excuses or implies they are not prioritizing their child's health
Fails to mention any public program or financial assistance option that may be available
model_answer: Thank you for explaining what has been going on, that helps me understand the situation better. It sounds like getting here for regular visits has been genuinely difficult with two jobs and no easy way to travel, and that is a real barrier, not a lack of care on your part. Let me ask, are you aware of any provincial or federal children's dental benefit program you might be eligible for? Many families qualify for coverage that pays for preventive visits and basic treatment, and our front desk can help you check eligibility today before you leave. In terms of making future visits more manageable, we could book your child's next cleaning as our very first appointment of the day so you are not waiting around, or we could try to schedule any siblings on the same day to reduce the number of trips you need to make. We can also set up a recall reminder by text message so you do not have to keep track of the date yourself. For today, let us treat the pain in tooth eight-four, and I will have the desk go over the cost and any coverage you may have. Does a first-appointment-of-the-day slot work better for your schedule going forward, and is there anything else that would make it easier for you to get your child in for care?

scenario_text: A 15-year-old competitive rugby player and their parent attend for a routine check-up. The clinical exam is unremarkable, but the history reveals the patient has never worn a mouthguard during games or practices, and the parent mentions the team does not require one.
task_instruction: Discuss the importance of a properly fitted mouthguard with the patient and parent and recommend an appropriate option.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions from the patient or parent
Gives the patient and parent the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses fees for a custom mouthguard
Discusses the patient's specific sport and level of contact if relevant

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains the risk of dental trauma (tooth fracture, avulsion, luxation) in contact sports without a mouthguard
Explains that a custom-fitted mouthguard offers better protection, fit, and comfort than a boil-and-bite or stock guard
Notes the mouthguard should be worn at every game and practice, not just games
Recommends a specific next step (taking impressions today or scheduling for a custom guard)
Verifies the patient and parent understand and agree with the recommendation

critical_errors: States that mouthguards are unnecessary because the team does not require one
Fails to recommend any mouthguard option at all
model_answer: I am glad we have a chance to talk about this today. Rugby is a high-contact sport, and even with good technique, a fall, a tackle, or an elbow to the face can fracture a front tooth, knock a tooth completely out, or push a tooth out of position, any of which can mean months of dental treatment and permanent changes to the smile. Right now you are not wearing any mouthguard, so every practice and game carries that risk. There are three main types available: stock guards you bite down on straight from the package, boil-and-bite guards you soften in hot water and mold yourself, and custom-fitted guards we make here from an impression of your own teeth. The custom option gives the best fit, the most even cushioning across your teeth, and it is also the most comfortable to talk and breathe through, which is why most athletes who try one stick with it. I would recommend we take an impression today so we can have your custom guard ready before your next practice, and I want to be clear this needs to be worn at every practice as well as every game, since a lot of injuries actually happen during regular training. We can go over the cost of the custom guard with you before you decide. Does this sound like the right option for you, and do you have any questions about caring for it or how long it should last?

scenario_text: A parent brings in their 6-year-old for a first dental visit. Examination shows deep occlusal grooves on the newly erupted first permanent molars, teeth 1.6, 2.6, 3.6, and 4.6, with no cavitation but plaque retained in the pits and fissures. The parent has never heard of sealants or fluoride varnish.
task_instruction: Explain fluoride varnish and dental sealants to the parent and recommend an appropriate preventive plan for the child.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the parent raises
Gives the parent the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses fees for the recommended preventive treatments
Discusses appropriate home care measures such as brushing technique

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains that the deep grooves on the first molars trap plaque and are difficult to clean with a toothbrush alone, increasing caries risk
Explains what a dental sealant is and how it physically seals the pits and fissures to prevent decay
Explains what fluoride varnish is and how it strengthens enamel and reduces caries risk
Recommends both sealants on the four permanent molars and periodic fluoride varnish application as an appropriate combined plan
Verifies the parent understands the recommendation and feels comfortable proceeding

critical_errors: States that sealants or fluoride varnish are unnecessary for a child with no cavities
Provides no preventive recommendation at all despite identifying the deep grooves
model_answer: Thank you for bringing your child in for this first visit, this is a great age to start preventive care. Looking at the four new adult molars that have come in at the back, teeth one-six, two-six, three-six, and four-six, I can see the chewing surfaces have deep natural grooves. Those grooves are so narrow that even careful brushing with a toothbrush cannot fully clean out the plaque that collects inside them, which is exactly the kind of surface where cavities commonly start in children this age. I would like to recommend two preventive treatments today. The first is a dental sealant, which is a thin protective coating we flow into those grooves and harden with a light, physically sealing out the bacteria and food that would otherwise get trapped there. The second is fluoride varnish, a concentrated fluoride treatment we paint onto all the teeth that soaks into the enamel and makes it more resistant to acid attacks; we would repeat this every few months as part of regular visits. Together, sealing the four new molars today and starting a varnish schedule gives your child strong protection right at the age when their risk of new cavities on these teeth is highest. We can also review brushing technique with your child to make sure the rest of the mouth stays clean between visits. I will have the front desk go over the cost of the sealants and varnish with you. Does this plan sound reasonable, and do you have any questions about how the sealants are placed or how long they typically last?

scenario_text: A patient requires a crown on tooth 3.6 following a large restoration failure. The patient's insurance plan covers only a portion of the cost, and the patient expresses frustration that they cannot afford the remaining balance, stating they may just leave the tooth as is.
task_instruction: Help the patient understand their insurance limitations and discuss realistic options for proceeding with care.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Acknowledges the patient's frustration without judgement
Discusses fees clearly and transparently

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Clearly explains what the insurance plan covers and what portion remains the patient's responsibility
Explains the clinical risk of leaving the tooth without a crown (further fracture, potential loss of the tooth)
Offers at least one practical alternative (a payment plan, a staged treatment approach, or a lower-cost interim restoration)
Avoids pressuring the patient and respects their right to decide
Verifies the patient understands the risks and benefits of each option discussed

critical_errors: Refuses to discuss any alternative options and insists the crown is the only acceptable treatment
Misrepresents what the insurance plan actually covers
model_answer: I can hear that this is frustrating, and I want to make sure you have all the information you need to make the right decision for yourself. Your plan is covering a portion of the crown, but there is a remaining balance that is your responsibility, and I understand that is a real financial concern. I do want to explain what happens if we leave the tooth without a crown right now. The remaining tooth structure on tooth three-six is weakened after the restoration failure, and without full coverage protection there is a real risk of the tooth cracking further under normal chewing forces, which could eventually mean losing the tooth altogether rather than restoring it. That said, you do have options besides paying the full remaining balance today. We could set up a payment plan so the cost is spread out over several months. Another option is placing a more affordable interim restoration now to protect the tooth and stabilize it, and planning for the crown once your finances allow, though I want to be honest that an interim restoration is not as durable long-term as the crown. It is entirely your decision how to proceed, and I am not going to pressure you either way, I just want you to understand the trade-offs. Which of these options feels more manageable for you right now, and do you have any questions about the risks of waiting or about how the payment plan would work?

scenario_text: A 52-year-old patient who smokes a pack of cigarettes daily and drinks alcohol most evenings attends for a routine recall. Intraoral examination reveals a white patch on the lateral border of the tongue that was not present at the previous visit.
task_instruction: Discuss the finding and the patient's oral cancer risk factors with them, and outline the next steps.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances if applicable
Discusses fees for any referral or follow-up

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Informs the patient of the new white patch (leukoplakia) found on examination in clear, non-alarming language
Explains that tobacco and alcohol use together substantially increase oral cancer risk
Recommends and offers referral for biopsy or specialist evaluation of the lesion
Offers smoking cessation resources or support without being judgemental
Verifies the patient understands the seriousness of prompt follow-up and the reasoning behind it

critical_errors: Fails to inform the patient of the new lesion found on examination
Tells the patient the lesion is definitely benign or definitely cancerous without appropriate referral for diagnosis
model_answer: During today's exam I found a white patch on the side of your tongue that was not there at your last visit, and I want to talk with you about it. This type of patch is called leukoplakia, and while many of these turn out to be harmless, some can be a sign of early changes that need to be checked by a specialist, so I do not want to leave this unaddressed. I also want to mention, since it is relevant to your risk, that using tobacco and drinking alcohol regularly together significantly increases the risk of oral cancer compared to either one alone, which is one of the reasons I want to be thorough about following up on this finding. My recommendation is that we refer you to an oral pathologist or oral surgeon for a biopsy so we can find out exactly what this patch is and get you the right treatment quickly if needed. I would also like to offer you some resources for cutting back or quitting smoking, not as a lecture, but because it is one of the most protective things you can do for your overall oral health going forward, and I can connect you with a cessation program if you are interested. I know this news can feel worrying, so I want to check in, do you have any questions about the biopsy process, what it involves, or about the smoking cessation resources? We can also go over what a referral visit typically costs before you leave today.

scenario_text: A pregnant patient in her second trimester attends for an emergency visit with swollen, bleeding gums. She mentions she has avoided dental care during pregnancy because she was told by a friend that dental treatment is unsafe while pregnant.
task_instruction: Discuss the safety of dental care during pregnancy and provide oral health promotion advice for this stage of pregnancy.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances (trimester, comfort, positioning)
Discusses fees for any recommended treatment

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Corrects the misconception, explaining that routine dental care including cleanings and necessary treatment is safe during pregnancy, particularly in the second trimester
Explains that pregnancy gingivitis is common due to hormonal changes and that good oral hygiene helps manage it
Recommends appropriate care now (a professional cleaning and periodontal evaluation) rather than delaying further
Verifies the patient feels reassured and understands the plan going forward

critical_errors: Confirms the misconception that dental treatment should be avoided during pregnancy
Fails to address the bleeding gums or provide any plan for the current visit
model_answer: I understand why you have been hesitant, but I want to reassure you that routine dental care, including cleanings, x-rays when needed, and necessary treatment, is safe throughout pregnancy, and the second trimester you are in right now is actually considered the most comfortable and ideal time to have dental work done. What you are experiencing with your gums, the swelling and bleeding, is very common in pregnancy and is often called pregnancy gingivitis. It happens because hormonal changes make your gums react more strongly to the plaque that is normally there, so even your usual brushing routine may not feel like it is enough right now. The good news is this is very manageable. I would like to do a professional cleaning today to remove the plaque and tartar buildup that is contributing to the inflammation, and we can go over some adjustments to your home care, like using a soft-bristled brush and possibly an antimicrobial rinse, to help keep things under control for the rest of your pregnancy. There is no need to delay any further visits out of concern for the pregnancy itself. Does this help put your mind at ease, and do you have any questions about the cleaning today or about caring for your gums between now and your next visit? We can also review the cost of today's cleaning before we begin.

scenario_text: A patient with type 2 diabetes attends for a recall visit. Periodontal charting shows generalized pocket depths of 5-6mm with bleeding on probing, and the patient mentions their blood glucose has been poorly controlled for the past several months.
task_instruction: Discuss the relationship between diabetes and periodontal health with the patient and promote a plan to address both.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances if applicable
Discusses fees for periodontal treatment

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains that diabetes and periodontal disease have a bidirectional relationship, each making the other harder to control
Explains that poor glycemic control increases susceptibility to periodontal breakdown
Explains that treating the periodontal disease may help improve glycemic control
Recommends periodontal therapy (scaling and root planing) and coordination with the patient's physician
Verifies the patient understands the connection and the recommended plan

critical_errors: Fails to mention any connection between the diabetes and the periodontal findings
Provides no periodontal treatment recommendation despite the findings
model_answer: I want to talk with you about how your diabetes and your gum health are connected, because they actually affect each other in both directions. When blood sugar is not well controlled, it makes it harder for your body to fight off the bacteria causing gum disease, which is likely part of why we are seeing these deeper pockets and bleeding today. At the same time, having active gum disease can make it harder to control your blood sugar, since the inflammation from periodontal infection can affect how your body responds to insulin. This means improving one can genuinely help the other. On our end, I would like to start periodontal therapy, specifically scaling and root planing to clean below the gumline and reduce the bacterial load and inflammation. This is likely to help reduce your pocket depths and bleeding over time. I would also suggest we coordinate with your physician or diabetes care team, since better glucose control will support the healing of your gums, and treating your gums may in turn help your overall glucose management. Does this connection make sense to you, and do you have any questions about the periodontal treatment or how it might interact with your diabetes management? I will also have the desk go over the cost of the scaling and root planing with you.

scenario_text: A patient in a wheelchair with limited hand mobility due to a motor disability attends for a recall visit. Examination reveals moderate plaque accumulation and early gingivitis, and the patient reports difficulty gripping a standard toothbrush.
task_instruction: Discuss adaptive oral hygiene strategies with the patient to promote better home care and disease prevention.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances (mobility, grip limitation)
Discusses fees for any recommended products

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies the grip limitation as the specific barrier to effective home care
Recommends an adaptive aid such as a built-up handle, modified grip, or an electric toothbrush
Discusses the option of caregiver-assisted brushing if appropriate for the patient's situation
Recommends adjunctive aids such as fluoride rinse or interdental cleaning tools suited to the patient's ability
Verifies the patient understands and feels the recommended strategies are practical for them

critical_errors: Recommends only standard oral hygiene instructions without addressing the stated grip limitation
Assumes the patient requires full caregiver care without first asking about their own abilities and preferences
model_answer: Thank you for letting me know that gripping a standard toothbrush has been difficult, that is really important for us to address so we can find something that actually works for you day to day. The plaque buildup and early gum inflammation I am seeing are consistent with the brush not being as effective as it could be, so let us look at some options. An electric toothbrush with a wide, easy-to-hold handle can make a big difference, since the brush head does most of the scrubbing motion for you and you mainly need to guide it along the teeth. If a manual brush is preferred, we can build up the handle with foam grip or an adaptive strap that wraps around your hand so you do not need a tight pinch grip to hold it. I also want to ask, is there a caregiver or family member who could assist with brushing on days when your hands feel more fatigued, purely as a backup rather than a replacement for your own routine? For cleaning between your teeth, a water flosser or a floss holder with a built-up handle may be easier to manage than traditional floss. Do any of these options sound like something that would realistically fit into your routine, and do you have any questions about how to use the electric brush or the floss holder? We can go over the cost of these products before you leave today.

scenario_text: A 68-year-old patient with a complete upper denture and a partial lower denture attends complaining of a persistent bad taste and mild discomfort under the upper denture. Examination reveals denture stomatitis and the patient admits to sleeping in the dentures every night and rarely cleaning them.
task_instruction: Educate the patient on proper denture care and hygiene to promote resolution of the condition and prevent recurrence.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances if applicable
Discusses fees for any recommended follow-up or antifungal treatment

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains that the condition (denture stomatitis) is commonly caused by wearing dentures continuously, including overnight, and inadequate cleaning
Recommends removing the dentures nightly to allow the tissue to rest and recover
Recommends a specific daily cleaning routine (brushing the dentures with a non-abrasive cleaner and soaking in an appropriate solution)
Recommends follow-up evaluation to confirm the tissue has healed and rules out the need for antifungal treatment
Verifies the patient understands the new routine and the reasoning behind it

critical_errors: Fails to mention removing the dentures at night as part of the recommended plan
Attributes the condition to a cause unsupported by the history without further discussion
model_answer: What you are describing, the bad taste and the discomfort under your upper denture, along with what I am seeing on examination, is called denture stomatitis, and it is a very common condition that develops when dentures are worn continuously, including overnight, combined with not cleaning them thoroughly each day. Essentially, the tissue underneath never gets a chance to rest, and bacteria and yeast can build up on the denture surface and irritate the gum tissue. The single most important change I would recommend is taking your dentures out every night before bed and leaving them out while you sleep, this gives the tissue time to recover and dramatically reduces the risk of this happening again. During the day, I would also like you to start brushing both dentures daily with a soft brush and a non-abrasive denture cleaner, never regular toothpaste since it can scratch the surface, and then soak them in a denture-cleaning solution overnight instead of wearing them. I would like to see you back in a couple of weeks to check that the tissue has healed with these changes; if it has not improved, we may need to consider a short course of antifungal treatment. Does this new nightly routine make sense, and do you have any questions about which cleaning products to use or how the follow-up visit will go? We can also discuss the cost if antifungal treatment ends up being needed.

scenario_text: A new immigrant family attends with their 9-year-old child for the first time. The parent explains that dental visits were not routinely available in their home country and that they are unfamiliar with the concept of preventive dental visits, believing dentists are only for emergencies.
task_instruction: Explain the value of preventive dental care to the family and promote establishing an ongoing relationship with the practice.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the parent raises
Gives the parent the opportunity to ask questions
Acknowledges the family's prior experience without judgement
Discusses fees for recommended preventive visits

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Acknowledges the family's prior experience and cultural context around dental care without judgement
Explains the concept and benefit of preventive care (catching problems early, preventing pain and costly treatment later)
Recommends a specific recall schedule appropriate for the child's age
Verifies the family understands and feels comfortable with the recommendation

critical_errors: Criticizes the family's prior lack of access to dental care or implies neglect
Fails to explain the concept of preventive care at all
model_answer: Thank you for sharing that with me, it makes a lot of sense that regular check-ups would feel like a new idea if dental visits where you are from were mainly for emergencies. I want to explain why we recommend visits even when nothing hurts, because I think it will help you see the value for your child. The idea behind preventive care is catching small problems, like an early cavity or a groove that is starting to trap plaque, before they turn into something painful or expensive to fix. A child who comes in regularly usually needs much less treatment overall than one who only comes in once something already hurts, because we can treat issues while they are still small or even stop them from becoming a problem at all through things like cleanings and fluoride. For your child's age, I would recommend a check-up and cleaning about every six months, so we can keep an eye on the new adult teeth coming in and catch anything early. There is no judgement here at all, plenty of families are new to this kind of routine care, and I am glad you have brought your child in today so we can start building that habit together. Does this explanation help make sense of why we recommend regular visits, and do you have any questions about what a typical check-up involves or what it costs? We are happy to go over the fees for a six-month recall schedule with you now.

scenario_text: A 40-year-old patient who plays recreational hockey attends for a check-up after chipping tooth 1.1 during a game last month, wearing no mouthguard. The patient states mouthguards feel bulky and they would rather just be careful.
task_instruction: Address the patient's reluctance and promote consistent mouthguard use going forward.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's specific concerns about comfort
Discusses fees for a custom mouthguard

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Acknowledges the patient's concern about bulkiness without dismissing it
Explains that the recent chip demonstrates real ongoing risk despite being careful
Explains that a custom-fitted mouthguard is thinner and more comfortable than stock alternatives, directly addressing the bulkiness concern
Recommends taking an impression for a custom guard today
Verifies the patient is now willing to consider consistent use

critical_errors: Dismisses the patient's comfort concern without offering any solution
Fails to recommend any mouthguard option after the patient's stated reluctance
model_answer: I hear you on the bulky feeling, that is one of the most common complaints people have about mouthguards, and it is a completely valid reason to have avoided wearing one before. At the same time, I want to point to what actually happened last month, you chipped tooth one-one during a game even while being careful, which tells me that being careful alone was not enough to prevent this injury, and the next impact could be worse, resulting in a cracked or knocked-out tooth rather than just a chip. The good news is the bulky feeling you are describing usually comes from stock or boil-and-bite guards, which are one-size-fits-all and often too thick or poorly fitted. A custom guard made from an impression of your own teeth can be trimmed much thinner in the areas that do not need extra protection while still being thick enough where it counts, so most patients find it far more comfortable to wear and even to talk through. I would recommend we take that impression today so you have a properly fitted guard ready before your next game. Would you be willing to give a custom guard a try given how much more comfortable it tends to be compared to what you may have tried before? We can go over the cost of the custom guard together, and I am happy to answer any other questions about wearing it during play.

scenario_text: A 25-year-old patient with a family history of early-onset periodontitis attends for a first visit at this practice. Clinical and radiographic examination is currently within normal limits, but the patient reports both parents lost most of their teeth to gum disease before age 45.
task_instruction: Discuss the patient's periodontal risk given their family history and outline a prevention-focused plan.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances if applicable
Discusses fees for a more frequent recall schedule

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains that a strong family history of early periodontitis is a recognized risk factor independent of current clinical findings
Reassures the patient that current findings are normal while explaining why closer monitoring is still warranted
Recommends a more frequent periodontal recall and monitoring schedule than standard
Discusses modifiable risk factors the patient can control (oral hygiene, smoking avoidance) to help offset genetic risk
Verifies the patient understands the increased risk and the recommended monitoring plan

critical_errors: Tells the patient their family history is irrelevant since current findings are normal
Recommends no change to the standard recall schedule despite the significant family history
model_answer: It is great that everything looks healthy today on your exam and x-rays, and I want to reassure you there are no signs of active gum disease right now. At the same time, what you have told me about both of your parents losing most of their teeth to gum disease before age forty-five is important information, because a strong family history like that is a recognized risk factor for developing periodontitis yourself, even independent of how healthy your gums look today. This does not mean it is inevitable for you, but it does mean I would like us to be more proactive than we would be for someone without that history. Rather than the standard once-a-year periodontal check, I would recommend seeing you every three to four months so we can closely monitor your gums and catch any early changes as soon as they appear, well before they would show up as visible disease. There are also things within your control that can help offset some of that genetic risk, particularly maintaining excellent daily oral hygiene, using an interdental cleaning tool consistently, and avoiding smoking, which significantly compounds periodontal risk when combined with a genetic predisposition. Does this plan make sense given your family history, and do you have any questions about the more frequent recall schedule or about what specific signs we will be watching for at each visit? We can also review the cost of the more frequent recall visits with you.

scenario_text: A teenage patient attends for a check-up accompanied by a parent. The patient mentions they recently started vaping and asks whether it is safer for their teeth and gums than smoking cigarettes, since several friends have told them it is completely harmless.
task_instruction: Provide accurate, evidence-based health promotion information to the patient about vaping and oral health.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient or parent raises
Gives the patient and parent the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances if applicable
Discusses cessation resources and their availability

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Corrects the misconception that vaping is completely harmless to oral health
Explains specific oral health effects associated with vaping (dry mouth, gum irritation, altered oral microbiome, potential effect on healing)
Encourages the patient to stop or avoid vaping and offers cessation support appropriate for a teen
Verifies the patient understands the information and communicates it in a non-judgemental, age-appropriate way

critical_errors: Confirms that vaping is harmless or safe for oral health
Lectures or shames the patient rather than providing factual information
model_answer: That is a good question to ask, and I am glad you brought it up rather than just going with what friends have said. Vaping is not harmless to your mouth, even though it does not involve burning tobacco the way cigarettes do. The vapor itself can dry out your mouth, and having less saliva means less natural protection against cavities and gum irritation. Vaping has also been associated with gum tissue irritation and changes to the bacteria that live in your mouth, and some early research suggests it may affect how well your gums heal if you ever need any dental treatment. So while it may carry somewhat different risks than cigarette smoking, calling it completely harmless would not be accurate. Since you are still fairly new to vaping, this is actually a good time to consider stopping before it becomes more of a habit, and I want you to know there is no judgement here, lots of teens try vaping without fully knowing these effects. If you are interested, there are cessation resources designed specifically for teens that can support you in quitting, and I am happy to connect you with those. Does this information change how you are thinking about vaping, and do you have any other questions about how it affects your teeth or gums? I am also happy to talk through any of this privately if that is more comfortable for you.

scenario_text: An elderly patient living alone attends for a recall visit and mentions they have been skipping meals and eating mostly soft, processed foods because chewing has become uncomfortable due to several missing posterior teeth. They have not considered replacing the missing teeth, believing it is too late at their age.
task_instruction: Discuss the impact of the missing teeth on the patient's nutrition and quality of life, and promote options for restoring function.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances (living alone, age)
Discusses fees for recommended restorative options

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains the connection between the missing posterior teeth, difficulty chewing, and the patient's reduced nutritional intake
Reassures the patient that age alone is not a barrier to restoring missing teeth
Discusses appropriate restorative options (partial denture, bridge, or implant depending on suitability) to restore chewing function
Highlights the potential improvement in nutrition and quality of life from restoring function
Verifies the patient understands the options and feels encouraged to consider treatment

critical_errors: Agrees that the patient is too old to benefit from tooth replacement
Fails to connect the missing teeth to the patient's dietary changes despite it being clearly reported
model_answer: I am glad you mentioned the changes to your eating, because I think what you are describing is directly connected to the missing back teeth, and I want to talk through some options with you. When the posterior teeth used for grinding and chewing are missing, it becomes much harder to break down firmer foods like meats, raw vegetables, and whole grains comfortably, which often leads people to shift toward softer, more processed foods, exactly what you have described. Unfortunately, that shift can mean missing out on important nutrients over time, which affects overall health and energy, not just dental health. I want to be clear that age is not a barrier to restoring these teeth, we regularly help patients in their seventies, eighties, and beyond regain the ability to chew comfortably again, it is truly never too late to consider this. Depending on the specific teeth missing and the condition of the surrounding bone and teeth, options could include a removable partial denture, a fixed bridge, or dental implants, each with different benefits, costs, and maintenance needs, and we can go through what would suit your specific situation. My hope is that restoring your ability to chew comfortably would let you return to a more varied, nutritious diet and make mealtimes something you look forward to again rather than something to work around. Does this change how you are thinking about replacing these teeth, and do you have any questions about which option might be the best fit for you? We can also review the costs of each option together.

scenario_text: A parent attends with their toddler for a first dental visit at 18 months of age, prompted by a public health nurse's referral. The parent reports the toddler still falls asleep with a bottle of milk most nights and asks whether this is a problem.
task_instruction: Discuss early childhood caries risk with the parent and promote appropriate feeding and hygiene practices.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the parent raises
Gives the parent the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the toddler's special circumstances if applicable
Discusses fees for any recommended follow-up

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains what early childhood caries is and how prolonged bottle feeding at night contributes to it
Recommends weaning the toddler off the nighttime bottle or switching it to water only
Recommends an age-appropriate home hygiene routine (wiping or brushing the toddler's teeth twice daily with an appropriate amount of fluoride toothpaste)
Recommends an appropriate recall schedule for continued monitoring
Verifies the parent understands the reasoning and feels able to implement the changes

critical_errors: States that the nighttime bottle habit poses no risk to the toddler's teeth
Fails to provide any recommendation on feeding or hygiene changes despite the parent directly asking
model_answer: Thank you for asking, this is an important thing to address early. Falling asleep with a bottle of milk most nights can lead to a condition called early childhood caries, sometimes called bottle rot, because the milk sugars sit on the teeth for long stretches while your toddler sleeps and there is very little saliva flow at night to wash them away, which lets cavity-causing bacteria thrive. This can affect the front teeth especially quickly and severely in young children. My main recommendation is to start weaning your toddler off the bottle at bedtime, and if a bottle is still needed to settle down, filling it with water only rather than milk or juice removes the sugar risk entirely. Alongside that, I would like you to start wiping or gently brushing your toddler's teeth twice a day, in the morning and right before bed, using a rice-grain-sized smear of fluoride toothpaste appropriate for this age. I would also recommend we see your toddler again in about six months so we can check how things are progressing and catch anything early if it does develop. Does this plan feel manageable to start at home, and do you have any questions about how to transition away from the nighttime bottle or about how much toothpaste to use? We are also happy to go over the cost of the next recall visit whenever you are ready to book.

scenario_text: A patient who works night shifts and struggles with an irregular sleep and meal schedule attends for a recall visit. Examination shows multiple new areas of early demineralization, and the patient reports frequently snacking on sugary energy drinks and chips to stay awake during shifts.
task_instruction: Discuss the patient's caries risk in the context of their lifestyle and promote realistic preventive strategies.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances (shift work schedule)
Discusses fees for recommended preventive products

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Identifies frequent sugary and acidic snacking during shifts as the primary contributor to the new demineralization
Acknowledges the challenge of maintaining routine hygiene with an irregular shift schedule without judgement
Suggests realistic substitutions or timing changes (water or sugar-free alternatives, limiting snacking frequency) that fit a shift-work schedule
Recommends a practical home fluoride measure appropriate for high caries risk
Verifies the patient feels the suggested changes are realistic given their schedule

critical_errors: Tells the patient to simply stop working night shifts as the primary solution
