Fails to identify any connection between the snacking pattern and the new demineralization findings
model_answer: Looking at your exam today, I am seeing several new areas of early demineralization, which are the earliest stage of tooth decay before an actual cavity forms, and I want to talk with you about what may be driving this. Based on what you have told me about your shifts, the frequent energy drinks and chips to stay awake are likely a major factor, since both the sugar and the acidity in those drinks create repeated attacks on your enamel throughout your shift, and unlike a regular meal schedule, this snacking pattern does not give your saliva much of a chance to neutralize the acid in between. I understand that working nights makes maintaining a typical routine difficult, and I am not suggesting you change your work schedule, just some adjustments that can realistically fit into it. Where possible, try swapping the energy drinks for water or a sugar-free alternative, and if you do have chips or a sugary drink, try to have it as part of one sitting rather than sipping or snacking continuously over your whole shift. I would also recommend using a fluoride mouth rinse or a higher-concentration fluoride toothpaste at night, since your risk level right now calls for extra protection. Do these suggestions feel realistic to fit into your shift routine, and do you have any questions about timing your snacks differently or about the fluoride products I mentioned? We can go over the cost of the prescription-strength toothpaste as well.

scenario_text: A patient recovering from treatment for oral cancer, including radiation to the head and neck, attends for a follow-up visit. The patient reports significant dry mouth and has noticed early demineralization on several teeth since completing radiation therapy six months ago.
task_instruction: Discuss the increased caries risk associated with radiation-induced xerostomia and promote an appropriate prevention plan.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances (cancer history, radiation effects)
Discusses fees for recommended prescription products

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains that radiation-induced xerostomia significantly increases caries risk due to reduced salivary protection
Recommends a prescription-strength fluoride regimen appropriate for this elevated risk level
Recommends saliva substitutes or stimulants to manage the dry mouth symptoms
Recommends a shortened recall interval for closer monitoring given the ongoing high risk
Verifies the patient understands the lifelong nature of this elevated risk and the importance of the preventive routine

critical_errors: Treats the patient's caries risk as equivalent to a patient without a history of head and neck radiation
Fails to recommend any specific preventive measure despite identifying the elevated risk
model_answer: I am glad you came in for this follow-up, and I want to talk with you about what we are seeing, the early demineralization on several teeth, in the context of your radiation treatment. Radiation to the head and neck can permanently reduce how much saliva your glands produce, and since saliva plays such a large role in washing away food debris, neutralizing acid, and helping repair early enamel damage, having significantly less of it puts you at a much higher, ongoing risk for new cavities compared to before your treatment. This is not a temporary risk that will resolve on its own, so we need to build a prevention plan around it for the long term. I would like to prescribe a high-concentration fluoride toothpaste or gel for daily use, since standard over-the-counter fluoride is usually not strong enough to protect teeth at this risk level. For the dry mouth itself, a saliva substitute spray or gel can provide symptomatic relief, and sugar-free lozenges or gum that stimulate saliva flow may also help if your glands still have some function remaining. Given how significant this risk is, I would also recommend we see you more frequently than a standard six-month recall, perhaps every three months, so we can catch and address any new areas as early as possible. Does this explanation help clarify why your risk is different now, and do you have any questions about the prescription fluoride or the saliva products? We can review the cost of the prescription items together as well.

scenario_text: A university student on a tight budget attends for a recall visit and mentions they have been using their roommate's leftover toothpaste and an old, badly frayed toothbrush because they cannot afford to buy their own oral care supplies right now.
task_instruction: Discuss affordable oral health promotion strategies with the patient given their financial constraints.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient raises
Gives the patient the opportunity to ask questions
Acknowledges the patient's financial constraints without judgement
Discusses fees for any products offered in-office

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Explains that a frayed toothbrush is significantly less effective at removing plaque and should be replaced
Offers a practical, low-cost solution (a free toothbrush and sample-size toothpaste from the office, or guidance on affordable options at a pharmacy)
Provides guidance on how often to replace a toothbrush going forward on a low budget
Verifies the patient feels comfortable with the suggested solution and no financial barrier remains for basic supplies

critical_errors: Dismisses the toothbrush condition as unimportant despite it being visibly frayed
Fails to offer any practical, low-cost solution despite the patient disclosing financial constraints
model_answer: Thank you for being upfront about that, it is really helpful for me to know so we can find a solution that actually works for your situation. I do want to mention that a badly frayed toothbrush loses a lot of its ability to clean effectively, since the bent, splayed bristles cannot get into the small spaces along the gumline and between teeth the way a fresh brush can, so this is worth addressing. The good news is we keep new toothbrushes and small sample tubes of toothpaste here at the office that we are happy to send home with you today at no cost, so that solves the immediate problem. Going forward, most pharmacies carry basic soft-bristled toothbrushes for just a couple of dollars, and a toothbrush generally should be replaced every three months or sooner if the bristles start to fray, so it does not need to be an expensive habit to maintain. Sharing toothpaste with a roommate is not a hygiene concern in itself, so that part is fine to continue if it helps with the budget. Does having a fresh brush and toothpaste from us today help take care of things for now, and do you have any questions about how to know when it is time to replace the brush again, or where to find affordable options later on?

scenario_text: A patient recovering from a stroke with residual weakness on one side of the body attends for a recall visit accompanied by their spouse. The spouse mentions the patient has been struggling to floss and brush thoroughly since the stroke, and plaque accumulation and gingival inflammation are notably worse than at the previous visit.
task_instruction: Discuss adaptive strategies to help the patient and spouse manage oral hygiene effectively given the patient's new physical limitations.
competent_behaviors: Answers any questions the patient or spouse raises
Gives the patient and spouse the opportunity to ask questions
Discusses the patient's special circumstances (stroke recovery, residual weakness)
Discusses fees for any recommended adaptive products

minimally_competent_behaviors.behavior: Connects the increased plaque and gingival inflammation to the patient's new difficulty performing thorough hygiene
Recommends an adaptive tool such as an electric toothbrush with a large handle or a built-up grip aid
Recommends an easier interdental cleaning alternative to string floss, such as floss picks or a water flosser
Discusses appropriate spouse or caregiver involvement in assisting with hygiene while respecting the patient's independence where possible
Verifies the patient and spouse understand and feel able to implement the suggested changes

critical_errors: Fails to acknowledge the connection between the residual weakness and the worsened plaque and gingival findings
Recommends only standard hygiene instructions with no adaptive strategies despite the stated limitation
model_answer: I can see from today's exam that plaque buildup and gum inflammation have both increased since your last visit, and given what you have shared about the residual weakness since your stroke, it makes sense that thorough brushing and flossing have become more difficult to manage the way you used to. Let us go through some adaptations that can help. An electric toothbrush with a large, easy-to-hold handle can make a real difference, since it requires less fine motor control to hold steady and the brush head does much of the cleaning motion for you; we can also add a foam grip or strap if holding it is still a challenge on the affected side. For cleaning between the teeth, traditional string floss can be quite difficult to manage one-handed, so I would suggest switching to floss picks, which only require one hand to use, or considering a water flosser, which many patients find easier to manage with limited dexterity. I also want to ask you both, would it be helpful for your spouse to assist with brushing or flossing on days when fatigue or weakness makes it harder to manage independently, while still letting you do as much as you comfortably can yourself? The goal is to keep your hygiene effective while respecting your independence as much as possible. Does this combination of tools and support sound workable for your daily routine, and do you have any questions about the electric toothbrush or the water flosser? We can review the cost of these products together as well.
